title: Electronics for Synth Builders
summary: Low-voltage DC electronics for building a synth: Ohm's law, dividers and pots, components, logic levels and datasheets, schematics and breadboards, measurement and soldering, and keeping audio quiet. No mains work.

lessons.title: Voltage, current and Ohm’s law
lessons.summary: Voltage is measured between two points; current passes through a component.
lessons.body:
Every circuit in a synth, from an LED on the front panel to the board's audio output, obeys a few simple rules. Learn them well now and the rest of this module is mostly applying them.

> [!warning] Low voltage only
> This module covers low-voltage DC work only: USB power, bench supplies of a few volts, and batteries. It does **not** cover mains wiring or mains power supplies. Use a ready-made, certified supply (a USB charger or a bench supply) and never open or modify anything that plugs into the wall.

## Four quantities
**Voltage** (written V, measured in volts, also V) is the difference in electrical potential between two points. It is the "push". A voltage is always *between* two points. "This pin is at 3.3 V" really means "3.3 V higher than ground".

**Electric current** ( written I, measured in amperes or amps, A) is the rate at which charge flows past a point. One amp is one coulomb per second. Current flows *through* things.

**Electrical resistance** ( written R, measured in ohms, Ω) is how strongly something opposes current. A resistor is a part made to have a known resistance.

**Electrical power** ( written P, measured in watts, W) is the rate at which energy is transferred, for example turned into heat in a resistor or into light in an LED.

A water analogy helps at first: voltage is pressure, current is flow rate, and resistance is a narrow pipe. Don't push it too far. It breaks down for capacitors and for anything at audio or radio frequencies.

## Ohm's law
Ohm's law is the rule you use most: it links the voltage across a resistor to the current through it. For an ohmic resistor at roughly constant temperature, the two are proportional. Double the voltage and the current doubles. The resistance is the fixed ratio between them:

```formula
V = IR
I = V / R
R = V / I
where
V: the voltage across the resistor, in volts (V); written after a number, V is the unit volt
I: the current through the resistor, in amperes (A)
R: the resistance, in ohms (Ω)
A: amperes (amps), the unit of current
Ω: ohms, the unit of resistance; 1 Ω passes 1 A when 1 V is across it
In words: voltage equals current times resistance. The second and third lines are the same law rearranged, so if you know any two of the three you can find the third.
```

For example, a 1 kΩ resistor (1000 Ω) with 5 V across it:

```formula
I = V / R
I = 5 V / 1000 Ω
I = 0.005 A = 5 mA
where
I: the current through the resistor, in amperes (A)
V: the voltage across the resistor, here 5 volts (V)
R: the resistance, here 1 kΩ = 1000 ohms (Ω)
A: amperes, the unit of current
mA: milliamperes; 1 mA = 0.001 A
Ω: ohms, the unit of resistance
In words: 5 volts across 1000 ohms drives 5 milliamps.
```

Ohm's law models ohmic resistors and the resistive part of wires when temperature and other conditions keep their resistance effectively fixed. It does not describe LEDs and diodes. Their current rises steeply with forward voltage rather than following a fixed resistance. Dividing voltage by current describes an operating point; it does not give a constant resistance that predicts another point. Apply Ohm’s law to the resistor in series with the LED, as in the neighbouring LED units.

## Key takeaways

- Voltage is measured between two points; current passes through a component.
- Use Ohm’s law for resistors at the stated operating conditions, not for LEDs.

## Further reading

- [OpenStax: Ohm’s law](https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-2/pages/9-4-ohms-law)
- [OpenStax: electric current](https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-2/pages/9-1-electrical-current)

questions.prompt: A 9 V battery is connected across a single 4.7 kΩ resistor. Roughly what current flows?

options.text: About 19 mA
options.explanation: This treats 4.7 kΩ as 470 Ω, a factor-of-ten prefix slip. 9 / 470 ≈ 19 mA, but the resistor is 4700 Ω.

options.text: About 42 A
options.explanation: This multiplies instead of dividing (9 × 4.7). Ohm's law finds current by dividing voltage by resistance, not multiplying them.

options.text: About 0.52 mA
options.explanation: This is R / V (4.7 / 9). The ratio is inverted; current falls as resistance rises.

options.text: About 1.9 mA
options.explanation: Correct. Current = voltage ÷ resistance = 9 V ÷ 4700 Ω ≈ 0.0019 A = 1.9 mA.

questions.workedExample:
1. Use Ohm's law in its current form and convert the prefix first: 4.7 kΩ = 4700 Ω.

```formula
I = V / R
I = 9 V / 4700 Ω
I ≈ 0.001915 A ≈ 1.9 mA
where
I: the current through the resistor, in amperes (A)
V: the battery voltage across the resistor, here 9 volts (V)
R: the resistance, here 4.7 kΩ = 4700 ohms (Ω)
A: amperes, the unit of current
mA: milliamperes; 1 mA = 0.001 A
Ω: ohms, the unit of resistance
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: 9 volts across 4700 ohms drives just under 2 milliamps.
```

2. Convert to milliamps by multiplying by 1000: 1.915 mA, about 1.9 mA.

Shortcut: volts ÷ kilohms gives milliamps directly, so 9 ÷ 4.7 ≈ 1.9 mA.

questions.prompt: You measure 2.5 mA through a resistor with 5 V across it. What is its resistance?

options.explanation: This multiplies 5 × 2.5, mixing a product with the units. Ohm's law finds resistance by dividing voltage by current.
This reverses the numerical ratio (2.5 ÷ 5 = 0.5) and treats milliamps as amps. Resistance is voltage divided by current after converting 2.5 mA to 0.0025 A.

options.text: 2 kΩ
options.explanation: Correct. Resistance = voltage ÷ current = 5 V ÷ 0.0025 A = 2000 Ω = 2 kΩ.
This is out by a factor of 10. 5 / 0.0025 = 2000.

questions.workedExample:
1. Convert the current: 2.5 mA = 0.0025 A.
2. Use Ohm's law in its resistance form:

```formula
R = V / I
R = 5 V / 0.0025 A
R = 2000 Ω = 2 kΩ
where
R: the resistance, in ohms (Ω)
V: the voltage across the resistor, here 5 volts (V)
I: the current through it, here 2.5 mA = 0.0025 amperes (A)
A: amperes, the unit of current
Ω: ohms, the unit of resistance
kΩ: kilohms; 1 kΩ = 1000 Ω
In words: a part that lets 2.5 milliamps through when 5 volts is across it has 2 kilohms of resistance.
```

Shortcut: volts ÷ milliamps gives kilohms: 5 ÷ 2.5 = 2 kΩ.

lessons.title: Resistor heat and an LED power budget
lessons.summary: Check resistor heat as well as current.
lessons.body:
Check resistor heat as well as current.

## Power: voltage times current
Power tells you how fast a part turns electrical energy into heat (or light). It's what decides whether a resistor survives. For a two-terminal part, instantaneous absorbed power is voltage times current when positive current enters the terminal labelled positive. In steady DC that is also the time-averaged electrical power. With changing signals, average the instantaneous product; multiplying arbitrary RMS voltages and currents is not a universal power rule:

```formula
P = VI
where
P: the power, in watts (W); 1 W is 1 joule of energy per second
V: the voltage across the part, in volts (V)
I: the current through the part, in amperes (A)
W: watts, the unit of power
In words: with the passive sign convention, voltage times current gives absorbed power. In this steady-DC example, 1 volt and 1 amp mean 1 watt; a negative result means the part supplies power.
```

For a resistor only, you can substitute Ohm's law into it. Replace V with I × R to get the second line, or replace I with V / R to get the third:

```formula
P = VI
P = (IR)I = I^2 R
P = V(V / R) = V^2 / R
where
P: the power the resistor turns into heat, in watts (W)
V: the voltage across the resistor, in volts (V)
I: the current through the resistor, in amperes (A)
R: the resistance, in ohms (Ω)
I^2: the current squared (multiplied by itself)
V^2: the voltage squared
W: watts, the unit of power
In words: all three lines give the same answer for a resistor. Use whichever matches the two quantities you know. Because current and voltage are squared, doubling either one quadruples the heat.
```

The squared forms only work for resistors, because they rely on Ohm's law. For a steady-DC LED, multiply its voltage by its current. A chip can have several supply and signal terminals; budget the relevant power flows rather than assuming one pair describes every path.

Power matters because resistors, regulators and chips all have a maximum they can dissipate before they overheat. A typical small through-hole resistor is rated at 0.25 W (check the actual part's datasheet).

> [!example] An LED's resistor
> A 5 V supply drives an LED through a 330 Ω resistor, and you measure 10 mA. How much voltage does the resistor take, how hot does it get, and what is left for the LED?

```formula
V_R = IR
V_R = 0.010 A × 330 Ω = 3.3 V
P_R = V_R I
P_R = 3.3 V × 0.010 A = 0.033 W = 33 mW
V_LED = V_supply − V_R = 5 V − 3.3 V = 1.7 V
where
V_R: the voltage across the resistor, in volts (V)
I: the current in the loop, here 10 mA = 0.010 amperes (A)
R: the resistor's resistance, here 330 ohms (Ω)
P_R: the power the resistor turns into heat, in watts (W)
V_LED: the voltage left across the LED, in volts (V)
V_supply: the supply voltage, here 5 V
V: volts, the unit of voltage
A: amperes, the unit of current
Ω: ohms, the unit of resistance
W: watts, the unit of power
mW: milliwatts; 1 mW = 0.001 W
In words: the resistor takes 3.3 V and makes 33 mW of heat, well inside a typical 0.25 W (250 mW) rating, and the remaining 1.7 V is across the LED.
```

The same sum as a short Python script:

```python
# LED budget on a 5 V supply
V_supply = 5.0
I = 0.010          # 10 mA
R = 330.0          # ohms

# Resistor drop; all current is in amps.
V_R = I * R        # Ohm's law
# Convert watts to mW only for display.
P_R = V_R * I      # P = VI
print(f"V across R: {V_R:.2f} V")
print(f"Power in R: {P_R*1000:.1f} mW")
V_led = V_supply - V_R  # KVL
print(f"Left for LED: {V_led:.2f} V")
```

```
V across R: 3.30 V
Power in R: 33.0 mW
Left for LED: 1.70 V
```

## Key takeaways

- Check resistor heat as well as current.
- The squared power formulas assume an ohmic resistor with a fixed resistance.

## Further reading

- [OpenStax: electrical energy and power](https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-2/pages/9-5-electrical-energy-and-power)
- [SparkFun: LED current limiting](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/light-emitting-diodes-leds/all)

questions.prompt: You put a 100 Ω, 0.25 W resistor directly across a 5 V supply. What happens, and what should you do?

options.text: Nothing to worry about: 50 mA is a small current
options.explanation: Small for a supply, maybe, but the resistor's power is what matters. 5 V × 50 mA = 0.25 W, right at the rating.

options.text: It dissipates 0.25 W, at its maximum rating, so it runs hot. Use a higher-wattage part or a larger resistance
options.explanation: Correct. Power = voltage² ÷ resistance = 25 ÷ 100 = 0.25 W. Running a part continuously at its rated continuous resistor dissipation under the specified thermal conditions is poor practice; leave margin (often half the rating or less) by using a 0.5 W part or a larger resistor.

options.text: It dissipates 2.5 W and burns out immediately
options.explanation: This multiplies voltage by resistance and divides by 10, or similar. Voltage squared ÷ resistance is 25 ÷ 100 = 0.25 W, not 2.5 W.

options.text: It dissipates 0.05 W, because power is voltage ÷ resistance
options.explanation: Voltage ÷ resistance is the current (0.05 A), not the power. Power is voltage × current.

questions.workedExample:
1. Find the current and the power:

```formula
I = V / R = 5 V / 100 Ω
I = 0.05 A = 50 mA
P = VI = 5 V × 0.05 A
P = 0.25 W
where
I: the current through the resistor, in amperes (A)
V: the supply voltage across it, here 5 volts (V)
R: the resistance, here 100 ohms (Ω)
P: the power turned into heat, in watts (W)
A: amperes, the unit of current
mA: milliamperes; 1 mA = 0.001 A
Ω: ohms, the unit of resistance
W: watts, the unit of power
In words: 5 volts across 100 ohms pushes 50 milliamps, which makes a quarter of a watt of heat.
```

2. Check with the resistor-only form:

```formula
P = V^2 / R
P = (5 V)^2 / 100 Ω
P = 0.25 W
where
P: the power in the resistor, in watts (W)
V: the voltage across it, here 5 volts (V)
R: the resistance, here 100 ohms (Ω)
V^2: the voltage squared, 5 × 5 = 25
Ω: ohms, the unit of resistance
W: watts, the unit of power
In words: voltage squared divided by resistance gives the same 0.25 W.
```

3. Compare with the rating: 0.25 W of 0.25 W, so 100%.
4. A resistor at its rated power can run hot; the permitted rating also depends on ambient temperature and mounting. Choose a 0.5 W part, or ask whether you really need that much current.

questions.prompt: Which statements about power in resistors are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Doubling the voltage across a fixed resistor quadruples its power
options.explanation: Correct. With resistance fixed, power is proportional to voltage squared. Doubling voltage therefore gives four times the heat.

options.text: For a fixed current, a larger resistor dissipates more power
options.explanation: Correct. At fixed current, resistor heat increases in proportion to resistance.

options.text: For a fixed voltage, a larger resistor dissipates more power
options.explanation: At fixed voltage, increasing resistance reduces current and dissipated power. What stays fixed matters.

options.text: The voltage-times-current power rule applies only to resistors
options.explanation: Instantaneous voltage times current gives absorbed power for a two-terminal part under the passive sign convention. The squared resistor formulas additionally require Ohm’s law.

questions.workedExample:
1. Fixed resistor, double the voltage:

```formula
P = V^2 / R
P_new = (2V)^2 / R = 4V^2 / R
where
P: the power in the resistor at the original voltage, in watts (W)
P_new: the power after doubling the voltage, in watts
V: the original voltage across the resistor, in volts (V)
R: the resistance, in ohms (Ω), unchanged
V^2: the voltage squared
In words: doubling the voltage multiplies the power by 2 × 2 = 4.
```

2. At fixed current, power scales with resistance because the same current-squared factor multiplies each resistance. For example, 10 mA through 100 Ω produces 0.01 W; through 200 Ω it produces 0.02 W.
3. At fixed voltage, power scales inversely with resistance because the squared voltage is unchanged. Example: 5 V across 100 Ω is 0.25 W; across 200 Ω it's 0.125 W.
4. Instantaneous voltage times current gives absorbed power for a two-terminal part when current enters its positive-labelled terminal. For steady DC it also gives time-averaged electrical power. Substituting Ohm's law gives the resistor-only forms.

lessons.title: Reading electronic units and prefixes
lessons.summary: Prefix case matters: milli and mega differ by a billion.
lessons.body:
Prefix case matters: milli and mega differ by a billion.

## Units and prefixes
Electronics spans huge ranges, so SI prefixes are everywhere. Get them wrong and you're off by a factor of a thousand.

| Prefix | Symbol | Factor |
|---|---|---|
| mega | M | 10⁶ |
| kilo | k | 10³ |
| milli | m | 10⁻³ |
| micro | µ (or u) | 10⁻⁶ |
| nano | n | 10⁻⁹ |
| pico | p | 10⁻¹² |

Tips:

- Note the case: **m** (milli) and **M** (mega) differ by 10⁹.
- Schematics often put the prefix where the decimal point would be (the RKM code, part of IEC 60062): `4k7` means 4.7 kΩ, `2R2` means 2.2 Ω, and `100n` means 100 nF.
- A handy pairing: volts ÷ kilohms = milliamps. 3.3 V across 1 kΩ is 3.3 mA.

## Key takeaways

- Prefix case matters: milli and mega differ by a billion.
- Read the unit before substituting a value into a calculation.

## Further reading

- [BIPM: SI prefixes](https://www.bipm.org/en/measurement-units/si-prefixes)
- [Vishay: resistor colour code](https://www.vishay.com/docs/49411/resistor_color_code_calculator.pdf)

questions.prompt: A schematic labels a capacitor `100n`. What value is that?

options.text: 0.1 µF
options.explanation: Correct. 100 nanofarads and 0.1 microfarads describe the same capacitance. Both forms appear on schematics and parts lists.

options.text: 100 µF
options.explanation: µ is 10⁻⁶ and n is 10⁻⁹. 100 µF would be a thousand times larger than 100 nF.

options.text: 100 mF
options.explanation: m (milli, 10⁻³) is a different prefix; 100 mF would be a huge capacitor and is a million times larger.

options.text: 100 pF
options.explanation: p is 10⁻¹², a thousand times smaller than n.

questions.workedExample:
1. `n` means nano, 10⁻⁹ (one billionth).
2. Convert to farads, then to microfarads:

```formula
C = 100 nF = 100 × 10^{-9} F
C = 10^{-7} F
C = 10^{-7} / 10^{-6} µF = 0.1 µF
where
C: the capacitance, in farads (F)
nF: nanofarads; 1 nF = 10^{-9} F
F: farads, the unit of capacitance
µF: microfarads; 1 µF = 10^{-6} F, a thousand nanofarads
10^{-9}: ten to the power minus 9, which is 0.000000001
In words: 100 nanofarads is the same amount as 0.1 microfarads, because a microfarad is a thousand nanofarads.
```

So 100n, 100 nF and 0.1 µF are the same part. This is the value commonly used for decoupling, which you will meet in the logic and datasheet units.

lessons.title: Complete loops and LED current
lessons.summary: A steady current needs a complete current return path.
lessons.body:
A steady current needs a complete current return path.

## Complete circuits
In the steady low-voltage DC model, sustained conduction current flows around a **closed electrical loop** (a complete circuit): from the supply's positive terminal, through the load, and back to the supply's negative terminal. Break the loop anywhere (an open switch, a loose jumper, a cracked solder joint) and the current everywhere in that loop drops to zero.

```diagram
 +5V ---[ R 330 ]---[ LED >| ]---+
  |                              |
 supply                          |
  |                              |
 0V -----------------------------+
          return path (ground)
```

Two consequences:

- **The current return path is part of the circuit.** A signal that leaves your synth board on one wire must come back on another. In ordinary unbalanced audio wiring, the sleeve or shield is that return; balanced audio uses a pair of signal conductors.
- **Current is the same everywhere in a single loop.** If 10 mA flows through the resistor, 10 mA flows through the LED. This is Kirchhoff's current law in its simplest form.

Kirchhoff's voltage law is the other half: around any closed loop, the voltage rises equal the drops. It's how you work out what is left for the LED once the resistor has taken its share:

```formula
V_supply = V_R + V_LED
5 V = 3.3 V + 1.7 V
where
V_supply: the voltage the supply raises, in volts (V)
V_R: the voltage dropped across the resistor, in volts
V_LED: the voltage dropped across the LED, in volts
V: volts, the unit of voltage
In words: going once round the loop, the voltage the supply provides is used up exactly by the parts in the loop. Nothing is left over and nothing is missing.
```

In this lumped, steady-DC model, include any significant wire resistance as another component. Kirchhoff’s laws do not require zero wire resistance. At high frequencies or with changing magnetic flux, the simple lumped model needs additional care.

## Conventional current and electron flow
Circuit diagrams and textbooks use **conventional current**: current flows from + to −. That convention predates the discovery of the electron. In a metal wire the charge carriers are actually electrons, which are negative and drift the opposite way, from − to +.

Both descriptions predict the same voltages, currents and power. Every formula, datasheet and schematic symbol uses conventional current. A forward-biased diode carries conventional current from anode to cathode (the bar). An LED's outward arrows indicate light, not current. Use conventional current and treat electron flow as a physics detail.

## Key takeaways

- A steady current needs a complete current return path.
- Use conventional current from anode to cathode through a forward-biased LED.

## Further reading

- [OpenStax: Kirchhoff’s rules](https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-2/pages/10-3-kirchhoffs-rules)
- [OpenStax: electric current](https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-2/pages/9-1-electrical-current)
- [SparkFun: LED current limiting](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/light-emitting-diodes-leds/all)

questions.prompt: For a battery driving a forward-biased LED through a resistor, which statement about conventional current and the LED symbol is correct?

options.text: From − to +, because the arrow follows the electrons
options.explanation: Electrons in a wire do drift from − to +, but schematics and formulas use conventional current, which goes the other way.

options.text: Conventional current flows through the load from + to − and through the LED from anode to cathode; its outward arrows show light
options.explanation: Correct. The cathode is marked by the bar; LED emission arrows describe light.

options.text: It doesn't matter, because AC and DC circuits use opposite conventions
options.explanation: The convention is the same for AC and DC. In AC the direction alternates, but the reference direction is still defined using conventional current.

options.text: The LED's outward arrows show electron flow
options.explanation: Those arrows show light emission. Electrons in metal move opposite conventional current.

questions.workedExample:
1. Conventional current is defined in the direction of positive-charge flow: through the external load from battery + to −.
2. In the forward-biased LED it flows from anode to cathode (the bar).
3. The LED symbol's small outward arrows represent emitted light. They are not current arrows.

questions.prompt: An LED circuit is: 3.3 V → 220 Ω resistor → red LED → ground. The LED datasheet gives a forward voltage of about 2.0 V at the current of interest. Approximately what current flows?

options.text: 15 mA
options.explanation: This is 3.3 V / 220 Ω, which ignores the voltage dropped by the LED. Only the resistor's share of the voltage sets the current through the resistor.

options.text: 9.1 mA
options.explanation: This is 2.0 V / 220 Ω. The resistor sees the supply minus the LED voltage, not the LED voltage.

options.text: It can't be estimated because LEDs don't obey Ohm's law
options.explanation: Ohm's law doesn't apply to the LED, but it does apply to the resistor. Using the LED's forward voltage gives a good estimate.

options.text: About 5.9 mA
options.explanation: Correct. The resistor has 3.3 − 2.0 = 1.3 V across it, so the current is 1.3 V ÷ 220 Ω ≈ 5.9 mA. The same current flows through the LED because it's a single loop.

questions.workedExample:
1. Kirchhoff's voltage law says the supply voltage is shared between the resistor and the LED. Find the resistor's share, then apply Ohm's law to the resistor only:

```formula
V_supply = V_R + V_LED
V_R = 3.3 V − 2.0 V = 1.3 V
I = V_R / R = 1.3 V / 220 Ω
I ≈ 0.0059 A ≈ 5.9 mA
where
V_supply: the supply voltage, here 3.3 volts (V)
V_R: the voltage across the resistor, in volts
V_LED: the LED's forward voltage, here about 2.0 V
I: the current in the loop, in amperes (A)
R: the resistor, here 220 ohms (Ω)
V: volts, the unit of voltage
A: amperes, the unit of current
mA: milliamperes; 1 mA = 0.001 A
Ω: ohms, the unit of resistance
≈: approximately equal to
In words: the LED takes about 2 V, the resistor gets the remaining 1.3 V, and 1.3 V across 220 Ω drives about 5.9 mA.
```

2. Single loop, so the LED carries the same 5.9 mA.

The real forward voltage shifts a little with current and temperature, so this is an estimate. Measure it to confirm.

questions.prompt: Your LED circuit works on the breadboard. You unplug the jumper that connects the LED's cathode back to ground. What is the current through the resistor now?

options.text: Zero, because the loop is broken
options.explanation: Correct. Current only flows around a complete loop. Breaking it anywhere, even on the ground side, stops current everywhere in that loop.

options.text: Unchanged, because the resistor is still connected to +3.3 V
options.explanation: Being connected to the supply at one end isn't enough. Without a current return path no charge can flow.

options.text: Higher, because the LED is no longer dropping voltage
options.explanation: Opening the loop stops steady current, so the resistor has no voltage drop. A voltage can still exist across the open gap or other nodes; removing the return does not bypass the LED.

options.text: Half, because only one side of the circuit is connected
options.explanation: Current isn't shared out by how many ends are connected. A loop is either complete or it isn't.

questions.workedExample:
1. Trace the loop: + → resistor → LED → jumper → ground → back to the supply.
2. Remove the jumper and the loop is open.
3. With an open loop, the current is zero everywhere in it.
4. A consequence: with no current, there's no voltage drop across the resistor, so both its ends and the LED's anode now sit at 3.3 V. A meter shows 3.3 V at the LED's anode, which can confuse you when debugging.

questions.prompt: A beginner connects an LED straight from a 3.3 V microcontroller pin to ground, with no resistor, reasoning that "3.3 V is low, so it's safe". Why is this a bad idea?

options.text: Above its forward voltage an LED's current rises very steeply, so nothing but the pin's internal resistance limits it. The current can exceed the pin's or LED's rating
options.explanation: Correct. An LED isn't a resistor. Once the voltage exceeds its forward voltage, a small extra voltage drives a big extra current. A series resistor sets the current.

options.text: LEDs need at least 5 V, so it simply won't light
options.explanation: Many LEDs, red ones especially, light well below 3.3 V. The risk isn't failure to light but too much current.

options.text: It's fine as long as the LED is red
options.explanation: Colour changes the forward voltage, but every LED has the same steep curve. Without a resistor the current is still uncontrolled.

options.text: The LED will reverse-bias and block all current
options.explanation: Connected anode to pin and cathode to ground, the LED is forward biased. Reverse bias is the wrong way round and is a different problem.

questions.workedExample:
1. Resistors obey Ohm's law: current is proportional to voltage.
2. LEDs and diodes don't. Near the forward voltage, current rises roughly exponentially with voltage.
3. With 3.3 V applied to a red LED with a nominal forward voltage of about 2 V, nothing sets the current except the pin driver's internal resistance and the LED's own resistance.
4. The resulting current can exceed the pin's maximum (see the board's datasheet) and the LED's rating.
5. Fix: a series resistor sized so that it takes the voltage the LED doesn't (the component units):

```formula
R = (V_supply − V_f) / I_LED
R = (3.3 V − 2.0 V) / 0.005 A
R = 260 Ω
where
R: the series resistor, in ohms (Ω)
V_supply: the pin's high voltage, here 3.3 volts (V)

I_LED: the LED current you want, here 5 mA = 0.005 amperes (A)

Ω: ohms, the unit of resistance
In words: the resistor gets the 1.3 V the LED doesn't use, and 1.3 V ÷ 5 mA is 260 Ω. Select the next larger preferred value, such as 270 Ω.
```

lessons.title: Ground references and return-wire voltage
lessons.summary: Circuit ground is a chosen reference, distinct from protective earth.
lessons.body:
Circuit ground is a chosen reference, distinct from protective earth.

## Ground is a reference
**Circuit ground** (GND, 0 V) is the point you choose to measure every other voltage against. In a battery- or USB-powered synth it's usually the supply's negative terminal. It doesn't have to connect to the earth in the soil.

Three meanings of "ground" get mixed up:

- **Signal or circuit ground:** the 0 V reference and current return path inside your circuit. This is what "GND" on a microcontroller board means.
- **Chassis ground:** the conductive case or chassis reference; whether it connects to circuit 0 V depends on the equipment design.
- **Protective earth:** the mains safety earth in a wall socket. It belongs to mains equipment and is not something to modify. The later noise and grounding units return to this.

Two practical rules follow:

1. **Direct, non-isolated single-ended signals need a common voltage reference.** For ordinary GPIO/UART links, connect the boards' GND pins. Isolated links such as DIN MIDI deliberately avoid a direct ground connection. A voltage only means something relative to a reference both sides agree on.
2. **"0 V" isn't the same everywhere.** Ground wires have small resistances. When current flows through them, two "ground" points can differ by a few millivolts. For audio that's enough to hear (the noise and grounding units).

## Key takeaways

- Circuit ground is a chosen reference, distinct from protective earth.
- Real return conductors develop voltage when current flows.

## Further reading

- [Analog Devices MT-031: converter grounding](https://www.analog.com/media/en/training-seminars/tutorials/MT-031.pdf)
- [RaneNote 110: system interconnection](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/note110.html)

questions.prompt: Which statements about ground are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ground is the reference point other voltages are measured against
options.explanation: Correct. "This pin is at 3.3 V" means 3.3 V relative to ground.

options.text: Two boards connected by ordinary non-isolated single-ended GPIO signals need a shared ground reference
options.explanation: Correct for this connection. Isolated interfaces such as DIN MIDI deliberately do not join their circuit grounds.

options.text: Ground in a USB-powered circuit must be wired to the earth pin of a wall socket
options.explanation: Circuit ground is just the 0 V reference, usually the supply's negative terminal. Protective earth belongs to mains equipment, which you should leave alone.

options.text: Every ground point in a circuit is at exactly 0 V at all times
options.explanation: Ground conductors have resistance. Current through them produces small voltage differences between "ground" points, which matters for audio.

questions.workedExample:
Check each statement against the lesson:

1. Reference: yes, by definition.
2. Shared ground: yes for ordinary direct single-ended GPIO; isolated links are an exception. A signal is a voltage relative to a reference. If two boards don't share one, the receiver measures against the wrong reference.
3. Earth pin: no. Circuit ground and protective earth are different things.
4. Exactly 0 V: no. Ground wires have resistance, so current through them leaves a small voltage:

```formula
V = IR
V = 0.1 A × 0.05 Ω = 0.005 V = 5 mV
where
V: the voltage between the two ends of the ground wire, in volts (V)
I: the current flowing in the wire, here 100 mA = 0.1 amperes (A)
R: the wire's resistance, here 0.05 ohms (Ω)
A: amperes, the unit of current
Ω: ohms, the unit of resistance
mV: millivolts; 1 mV = 0.001 V
In words: a ground wire of a twentieth of an ohm carrying 100 mA has 5 millivolts across it, so its two ends are not both at exactly 0 V.
```

options.text: 2 mV

questions.workedExample:
1. The return current flows through the ground wire's resistance, so Ohm's law gives the voltage across the wire:

```formula

V = 0.2 A × 0.05 Ω
V = 0.01 V = 10 mV
where
V: the voltage between board A's ground and board B's ground, in volts (V)
I: the return current in the ground wire, here 200 mA = 0.2 amperes (A)
R: the ground wire's resistance, here 0.05 ohms (Ω)

mV: millivolts; 1 mV = 0.001 V

```

2. Board A's ground is therefore 10 mV away from board B's.
3. B measures A's signal plus or minus that 10 mV.

For a logic signal with volts of margin this doesn't matter. For audio it does. A changing return current, such as a processor's or LED's, puts its pattern into the audio as noise. The noise units cover fixes.

lessons.title: Combining series and parallel resistors
lessons.summary: Series resistances add; parallel branches share a voltage.
lessons.body:
A common analogue knob on a microcontroller synth uses a potentiometer as a voltage divider. The board reads its wiper voltage with an ADC and turns it into a number; encoders and other controls work differently. To wire knobs correctly, and to understand why some readings come out wrong, you need series and parallel resistance and the divider formula.

## Series: one path, resistances add
Components in **series** (a series circuit) share a single current path. The same current flows through each one, and their voltages add up to the total. Because the current has to push through every resistor in turn, their resistances simply add:

```formula
R_total = R1 + R2 + R3 + ...
where
R_total: the single resistance that behaves the same as the whole chain, in ohms (Ω)
R1: the first resistor in the chain, in ohms
R2: the second resistor, in ohms
R3: the third resistor, in ohms
...: and so on, for as many resistors as are in the chain
Ω: ohms, the unit of resistance
In words: resistors in series add up. The total is always larger than the largest one.
```

For example, a 1 kΩ and a 2.2 kΩ in series:

```formula
R_total = R1 + R2
R_total = 1 kΩ + 2.2 kΩ = 3.2 kΩ
where
R_total: the combined resistance, in ohms (Ω)
R1: the first resistor, here 1 kΩ
R2: the second resistor, here 2.2 kΩ
kΩ: kilohms; 1 kΩ = 1000 ohms (Ω)
In words: the pair behaves exactly like one 3.2 kΩ resistor.
```

## Parallel: several paths, conductances add
Components in **parallel** (a parallel circuit) connect across the same two connection points, so they all have the **same voltage**. The currents split between the branches and add up to the total. Each extra branch is another path for current, so the combination conducts *more* easily than any branch alone.

The easy way to add them is by **conductance**, which is one divided by resistance (how easily current flows). Conductances in parallel add:

```formula
1 / R_total = 1 / R1 + 1 / R2 + ...
where
R_total: the single resistance that behaves the same as all the branches together, in ohms (Ω)
R1: the first branch's resistance, in ohms
R2: the second branch's resistance, in ohms
...: and so on, one term per branch
Ω: ohms, the unit of resistance
In words: add up one-over-resistance for every branch, then take one over the answer. Each branch adds a path, so the total always comes out smaller than the smallest branch.
```

For exactly two resistors this rearranges into a handier "product over sum" form. The symbol ∥ is shorthand for "in parallel with":

```formula
R1 ∥ R2 = (R1 R2) / (R1 + R2)
where
R1 ∥ R2: the combined resistance of R1 and R2 in parallel, in ohms (Ω)
∥: "in parallel with"
R1: the first resistor, in ohms
R2: the second resistor, in ohms
Ω: ohms, the unit of resistance
In words: for two resistors in parallel, multiply them, then divide by their sum.
```

Three facts are worth memorising:

- Two equal positive resistors in parallel give half the value: two 10 kΩ parts combine to 5 kΩ.
- The parallel total is always **smaller than the smallest** branch.
- A much larger resistor in parallel barely changes anything:

```formula
10 kΩ ∥ 1 MΩ = (10 kΩ × 1000 kΩ) / 1010 kΩ
10 kΩ ∥ 1 MΩ ≈ 9.9 kΩ
where
∥: "in parallel with"
kΩ: kilohms; 1 kΩ = 1000 ohms (Ω)
MΩ: megohms; 1 MΩ = 1000 kΩ = 1,000,000 Ω
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: putting a 1 MΩ resistor across a 10 kΩ one lowers it by only about 1%, because almost all the current takes the easier 10 kΩ path.
```

## Key takeaways

- Series resistances add; parallel branches share a voltage.
- For positive finite resistances, a parallel total is below the smallest branch.

## Further reading

- [OpenStax: series and parallel resistors](https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-2/pages/10-2-resistors-in-series-and-parallel)

lessons.title: Deriving an unloaded voltage divider
lessons.summary: The output is the bottom resistor’s share of the input.
lessons.body:
The output is the bottom resistor’s share of the input.

## The voltage divider
Two resistors in series across a supply split the voltage in proportion to their resistances. The output is taken from the junction:

```diagram
 Vin ──┐
       R1
       ├──── Vout
       R2
 GND ──┘
```

The formula comes straight from the two laws in the voltage and current units. The resistors are in series, so one current flows through both, set by their total. Ohm's law on R2 alone then gives the voltage across it:

```formula
I = Vin / (R1 + R2)
Vout = I × R2
Vout = Vin R2 / (R1 + R2)
where
I: the current flowing down through both resistors, in amperes (A)
Vin: the input (supply) voltage across the whole divider, in volts (V)
Vout: the output voltage, measured from the junction to ground, in volts
R1: the top resistor, between Vin and the output, in ohms (Ω)
R2: the bottom resistor, between the output and ground, in ohms
In words: the output is the input voltage scaled by the bottom resistor's share of the total resistance. This holds only when nothing draws current from the output.
```

Two examples:

```formula
Vout = 3.3 V × 10 kΩ / (10 kΩ + 10 kΩ)
Vout = 3.3 V × 0.5 = 1.65 V
Vout = 5 V × 10 kΩ / (20 kΩ + 10 kΩ)
Vout = 5 V × 1/3 ≈ 1.67 V
where
Vout: the divider's unloaded output, in volts (V)
V: volts, the unit of voltage
kΩ: kilohms; 1 kΩ = 1000 ohms
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: two equal resistors halve the voltage. With 20 kΩ on top and 10 kΩ below, the bottom resistor is a third of the total, so you get a third of the 5 V.
```

The ratio sets the output, not the individual resistance values. 1 kΩ/1 kΩ and 100 kΩ/100 kΩ both halve the voltage when unloaded.

The individual resistance values still matter in two ways. They set the divider standing current (and so the wasted power), and they determine how badly the output sags when something draws current from it.

## Key takeaways

- The output is the bottom resistor’s share of the input.
- An unloaded ratio says nothing about how well a divider drives a load.

## Further reading

- [SparkFun: voltage dividers](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/voltage-dividers/all)
- [OpenStax: series and parallel resistors](https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-2/pages/10-2-resistors-in-series-and-parallel)

This is the voltage across the *top* resistor (5 V × 20/30). The output is the voltage across the bottom resistor.

A resistive divider can never output more than its input. This is 5 × 20/10, an inverted ratio.


lessons.title: Loading, source resistance and divider limits
lessons.summary: Combine a resistive load with the bottom resistor first.
lessons.body:
Combine a resistive load with the bottom resistor first.

## Loading: the divider's output changes when you use it
The divider formula assumes nothing draws current from the output. Anything you connect there is a **load** (an electrical load), and it sits in parallel with the bottom resistor. That lowers the effective bottom resistance, so the output falls. To find the loaded output, combine the load with the bottom resistor first, then use the divider formula as before:

```formula
R2_eff = R2 ∥ R_load
Vout = Vin R2_eff / (R1 + R2_eff)
where
R2_eff: the effective bottom resistance with the load attached, in ohms (Ω)
R2: the bottom resistor, in ohms
R_load: the resistance of whatever is connected to the output, in ohms
∥: "in parallel with", worked out as (a × b) / (a + b)
Vout: the loaded output voltage, in volts (V)
Vin: the input voltage, in volts
R1: the top resistor, in ohms
In words: a load in parallel with the bottom resistor makes it look smaller, so the output voltage falls.
```

For a 10 kΩ/10 kΩ divider from 3.3 V with a 10 kΩ load:

```formula
R2_eff = 10 kΩ ∥ 10 kΩ = 5 kΩ
Vout = 3.3 V × 5 kΩ / (10 kΩ + 5 kΩ)
Vout = 1.1 V
where
R2_eff: the bottom resistor with the load in parallel
Vout: the loaded output voltage
∥: "in parallel with"
kΩ: kilohms; 1 kΩ = 1000 ohms
V: volts, the unit of voltage
In words: a load equal to the bottom resistor drags the output from 1.65 V down to 1.1 V, a third lower.
```

The script below repeats this for several loads:

```python
# Both input resistances are in ohms.
def par(a, b):
    return a * b / (a + b)

def divider(vin, r1, r2):
    return vin * r2 / (r1 + r2)

vin, r1, r2 = 3.3, 10e3, 10e3
v0 = divider(vin, r1, r2)
print(f"unloaded: {v0:.3f} V")
for load in (1e6, 100e3, 10e3, 1e3):
    # The load shunts the lower resistor.
    v = divider(vin, r1, par(r2, load))
    k = load / 1e3
    print(f"load {k:>6.0f}k: {v:.3f} V")
```

```
unloaded: 1.650 V
load   1000k: 1.642 V
load    100k: 1.571 V
load     10k: 1.100 V
load      1k: 0.275 V
```

For a resistive load, compare it with the divider’s output resistance and your allowed error: a load ten times that resistance causes about 9.1% sag, while a hundred times causes about 1% sag. These are trade-offs, not universal pass/fail limits. A 1 MΩ load barely moves a 10 kΩ divider. A 10 kΩ load drags it from 1.65 V to 1.10 V.

The divider's **output resistance** (its source impedance) tells you how easily a load can pull it around. Seen from the output, the supply acts like a short for changes, so the two resistors appear in parallel:

```formula
R_out = R1 ∥ R2 = (R1 R2) / (R1 + R2)
R_out = (10 kΩ × 10 kΩ) / 20 kΩ = 5 kΩ
where
R_out: the divider's output resistance, in ohms (Ω)
R1: the top resistor, here 10 kΩ
R2: the bottom resistor, here 10 kΩ
∥: "in parallel with"
kΩ: kilohms; 1 kΩ = 1000 ohms (Ω)
In words: the divider behaves like a perfect voltage source with 5 kΩ in series. Loads much larger than 5 kΩ barely move it.
```

The lower the output resistance, the less a load disturbs it, but the more **divider standing current** (the current that flows through the divider all the time) it wastes.

> [!note] Why this matters for ADCs
> A microcontroller's ADC input isn't a pure open circuit. Many ADCs briefly connect a small sampling capacitor that has to charge through the source's resistance. If the source impedance is too high, the sampling capacitor may not settle to the new input voltage; the error can have either sign depending on its previous charge, and noise can also matter. The chip's datasheet or reference manual states the maximum source impedance for a given sampling time. Check it for your board rather than assuming a value.

### Dividers are not power supplies

A divider can make a reference voltage for a high-impedance input. It can't power anything that draws significant or varying current. Feed a 5 V-to-3.3 V divider into a board's power pin and the voltage collapses as soon as the board draws current. Use a voltage regulator for power.

## Key takeaways

- Combine a resistive load with the bottom resistor first.
- Output resistance and allowed error determine acceptable loading.

## Further reading

- [TI: linear-regulator fundamentals](https://www.ti.com/video/series/power-fundamentals-linear-regulator-fundamentals.html)

- [SparkFun: voltage dividers](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/voltage-dividers/all)
- [OpenStax: series and parallel resistors](https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-2/pages/10-2-resistors-in-series-and-parallel)

```formula
V: volts
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: the illustrative low-resistance dummy load swamps the bottom resistor, so almost all of the 5 V is lost across the top resistor and the illustrative resistive load gets about a sixth of a volt. A real board needs its own current-versus-voltage model.
```

4. The board won't run, and as its current changes so does the voltage.
5. A regulator actively holds its output constant as load current changes. That's the right part for power.

questions.prompt: A divider must give about 1.0 V from 3.3 V for a reference input whose input resistance is around 1 MΩ. Which choice is best, and why?

options.text: 2.3 Ω on top, 1 Ω below: lowest output resistance
options.explanation: The ratio is right, but 3.3 V across 3.3 Ω draws 1 A and wastes 3.3 W. That's absurd for a reference.

options.text: 2.3 MΩ on top, 1 MΩ below: lowest power
options.explanation: The power is tiny, but the 1 MΩ load is now in parallel with the 1 MΩ bottom resistor, halving it. The output falls to about 0.59 V.

options.text: 23 kΩ on top, 10 kΩ below: right ratio, the 1 MΩ load is about 140× the ~7 kΩ output resistance, and the divider standing current is only 0.1 mA
options.explanation: Correct. Unloaded output: 3.3 V × 10 ÷ 33 = 1.0 V. Output resistance: 23 kΩ ∥ 10 kΩ ≈ 7 kΩ, so the 1 MΩ load shifts the output by under 1%. Divider standing current: 3.3 V ÷ 33 kΩ = 0.1 mA.

options.text: Any pair with a 2.3:1 ratio works equally well
options.explanation: Only for an unloaded divider. With a real load, individual resistance values decide how much the output sags and how much power is wasted.

questions.workedExample:
1. Find the ratio the divider needs:

```formula
Vout / Vin = R2 / (R1 + R2)
1.0 V / 3.3 V ≈ 0.303
R1 ≈ 2.3 × R2
where
Vout: the wanted output, here 1.0 volts (V)
Vin: the supply, here 3.3 V
R1: the top resistor, in ohms (Ω)
R2: the bottom resistor, in ohms
V: volts
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: the bottom resistor must be about 30% of the total, which means the top one is about 2.3 times the bottom one.
```

2. Check loading for the two serious options. The 1 MΩ input sits in parallel with the bottom resistor:

```formula
R2_eff = 1 MΩ ∥ 10 kΩ ≈ 9.90 kΩ
Vout = 3.3 V × 9.90 / 32.9 ≈ 0.993 V
R2_eff = 1 MΩ ∥ 1 MΩ = 0.5 MΩ
Vout = 3.3 V × 0.5 / 2.8 ≈ 0.59 V
where
R2_eff: the bottom resistor with the 1 MΩ input in parallel; the first two lines are the 23 kΩ/10 kΩ pair (total 23 + 9.90 = 32.9 kΩ), the last two the 2.3 MΩ/1 MΩ pair (total 2.3 + 0.5 = 2.8 MΩ)
∥: "in parallel with": (a × b) / (a + b)
Vout: the loaded output voltage, in volts (V)
kΩ: kilohms; 1 kΩ = 1000 ohms
MΩ: megohms; 1 MΩ = 1000 kΩ
V: volts
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: with 23 kΩ and 10 kΩ the load barely matters (0.993 V instead of 1.0 V); with 2.3 MΩ and 1 MΩ it halves the bottom resistor and the output falls to 0.59 V.
```

3. Check power: 23 kΩ + 10 kΩ draws 3.3 V ÷ 33 kΩ = 0.1 mA (0.33 mW). The 3.3 Ω pair draws 1 A.
4. Middle values balance loading against waste.

lessons.title: Wiring a potentiometer to an ADC
lessons.summary: Use the documented analogue supply and ADC voltage limits.
lessons.body:
Use the documented analogue supply and ADC voltage limits.

## The potentiometer: a divider with a moving tap
A **potentiometer** (pot) is a resistive track with a wiper that slides along it. It has three terminals: the two ends of the track and the wiper.

```diagram
  pin 1 ──/\/\/\/\/\/\── pin 3
              ↑
           pin 2 (wiper)
```

Wire one end to the supply, the other to ground, and the wiper is a divider output. Turn the knob and you move the wiper position between the upper part of the track and the lower part. The total stays fixed:

```formula
R_top + R_bottom = R_pot
V_wiper = Vin R_bottom / R_pot
where
R_top: the track resistance between the supply end and the wiper, in ohms (Ω)
R_bottom: the track resistance between the wiper and the ground end, in ohms
R_pot: the pot's total (end-to-end) resistance, in ohms, e.g. 10 kΩ
V_wiper: the voltage on the wiper, measured to ground, in volts (V)
Vin: the voltage across the whole track, in volts
In words: the two parts of the track always add up to the pot's value, and the wiper voltage is the input scaled by the lower part's share.
```

For an unloaded linear 10 kΩ pot across 3.3 V, a quarter-track setting leaves 2.5 kΩ below the wiper and gives about 0.83 V. This assumes the ground end is the bottom and the track is ideal.

For a microcontroller knob:

```diagram
 3.3V ── pin 3
        pot track ── pin 2 ── ADC pin
 GND ── pin 1
```

Points to watch:

- **Use the board's documented analogue supply for the pot, matching the ADC range.** Do not load an unbuffered VREF pin unless the documentation explicitly allows it. If the pot is fed from a different voltage, the ADC's full range won't match the knob's full range. Feeding it from a higher voltage could also exceed the input's maximum (the logic and datasheet units).
- **Swapping pins 1 and 3** reverses the direction of the knob. It's harmless and easily fixed in software.
- **Never wire the wiper straight to a supply rail.** At one extreme the wiper sits at the end connected to ground, and you'd short the supply through a few ohms of track.
- **The pot's resistance** trades divider standing current against source impedance. Values around 10 kΩ are a common choice for microcontroller knobs, but confirm against the ADC's source-impedance limit.

## Worst-case source resistance

```formula
R_bottom = x R_pot
R_top = (1 − x)R_pot
R_out = R_pot x(1 − x)
R_out ≤ R_pot / 4
R_out = 100 kΩ / 4 = 25 kΩ
where
R_bottom: track resistance from wiper to ground, in ohms (Ω)
R_top: track resistance from supply to wiper, in ohms
R_pot: total ideal linear-track resistance, in ohms; 100 kΩ in the last line
x: fraction of the track below the wiper, between zero and one
R_out: unloaded wiper source resistance, in ohms; the last line is at mid-track
≤: less than or equal to
kΩ: kilohms, one thousand ohms
In words: The two track segments appear in parallel to a load. Their product is largest at mid-track, so a 100 kΩ pot can present 25 kΩ to the ADC. Do not assume that meets the ADC acquisition-time requirement.
```

## Key takeaways

- Use the documented analogue supply and ADC voltage limits.
- A pot’s wiper source resistance peaks in the middle of a linear track.

## Further reading

- [Bourns PDB181-GTR: circuit and taper charts](https://www.bourns.com/docs/product-datasheets/PDB181-GTR.pdf)
- [SparkFun: voltage dividers](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/voltage-dividers/all)
- [PJRC: Teensy 4.1 signal-voltage limits](https://www.pjrc.com/store/teensy41.html)

questions.prompt: A pot is wired with one end to 3.3 V, the other end to ground, and the wiper to an ADC pin. What does turning the knob change?

options.text: The total resistance between 3.3 V and ground
options.explanation: The track between the two ends is fixed. Only the wiper's position on it changes.

options.text: The ratio of the two parts of the track, and so the divider's output voltage
options.explanation: Correct. The wiper splits the fixed track into an upper part and a lower part. Their ratio sets the wiper voltage, from 0 V to 3.3 V.

options.text: The current drawn from the supply, from zero to maximum
options.explanation: The current through the track is 3.3 V divided by the pot's total resistance, which is constant whatever the wiper position (ignoring the ADC's tiny load).

options.text: The ADC's reference voltage
options.explanation: The reference is fixed by the board. The pot produces a voltage between 0 V and its top end, which the ADC measures against that reference.

questions.workedExample:
1. The two ends of the track connect to 3.3 V and 0 V, so the full 10 kΩ (say) is always across the supply.
2. The wiper divides the track into an upper and a lower part that always add up to 10 kΩ:

```formula
R_top + R_bottom = 10 kΩ
V_wiper = 3.3 V × R_bottom / 10 kΩ
I = 3.3 V / 10 kΩ = 0.33 mA
where
R_top: the track between the 3.3 V end and the wiper, in kilohms (kΩ)
R_bottom: the track between the wiper and ground, in kilohms
V_wiper: the wiper voltage, measured to ground, in volts (V)
I: the current through the whole track, in milliamps (mA)
kΩ: kilohms; 1 kΩ = 1000 ohms
V: volts
mA: milliamperes; 1 mA = 0.001 amperes
In words: turning the knob changes how the fixed 10 kΩ is split, which sweeps the wiper from 0 V to 3.3 V, while the current through the track never changes.
```

3. So rotation changes only the ratio, and with it the output voltage.

questions.prompt: Your ADC's datasheet limits the source impedance to a few kilohms for the sampling time you've chosen. You're reading a 100 kΩ linear pot wired as a divider. At what wiper position is its source impedance highest, and what is it?

options.text: At either end, 100 kΩ
options.explanation: At the ends one part of the track is 0 Ω, so the source impedance is about 0 Ω, its lowest.

options.text: At mid-rotation, 50 kΩ
options.explanation: 50 kΩ is each half, but the two halves are in parallel as seen from the wiper, which gives 25 kΩ.

options.text: It's constant at 100 kΩ
options.explanation: The end-to-end resistance is constant, but the impedance seen at the wiper depends on position.

options.text: At mid-rotation, 25 kΩ
options.explanation: Correct. The source impedance is the upper and lower parts of the track in parallel. At mid-rotation that's 50 kΩ ∥ 50 kΩ = 25 kΩ, the maximum, and well above a few kilohms.

questions.workedExample:
1. Seen from the wiper, the upper and lower parts of the track are in parallel (the supply counts as a short for changes).
2. Describe the wiper position by the fraction of the track below it and work out that parallel combination:

```formula
R_bottom = xR
R_top = (1 − x)R
Z = R_top ∥ R_bottom = Rx(1 − x)
Z_max = R × 0.5 × 0.5 = R / 4
Z_max = 100 kΩ / 4 = 25 kΩ
where
R: the pot's total track resistance, here 100 kΩ
x: the fraction of the track below the wiper, from 0 (at the ground end) to 1 (at the top)
R_bottom: the track between the wiper and ground, in kilohms (kΩ)
R_top: the track between the wiper and the supply, in kilohms
Z: the source impedance seen at the wiper, in kilohms
Z_max: the largest value Z reaches, at x = 0.5
∥: "in parallel with": (a × b) / (a + b)
kΩ: kilohms; 1 kΩ = 1000 ohms
In words: the source impedance is zero at either end and peaks at a quarter of the pot's value when the knob is in the middle.
```

3. At either ideal track end, the source resistance approaches zero, because one part of the track has no resistance.
4. Fixes: use a lower-value pot (10 kΩ peaks at 2.5 kΩ), lengthen the sampling time, or add a small capacitor or buffer at the ADC pin, checking your chip's documentation for which is recommended.

questions.prompt: Which statements about wiring a pot to a microcontroller are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Swapping the two end pins reverses the knob's direction but is otherwise harmless
options.explanation: Correct. It mirrors the divider, and you can invert it in software if you prefer.

options.text: Connecting the wiper directly to 3.3 V and one end to ground risks shorting the supply when the knob is at that end
options.explanation: Correct. At that extreme the wiper sits on the grounded end, connecting 3.3 V to ground through almost zero track resistance.

options.text: Feed the pot from the documented analogue supply matching the ADC range, with its wiper always within the input-voltage limits
options.explanation: Correct. Match the documented input range and supply limits. Do not load an unbuffered VREF pin unless its documentation permits it.

options.text: Feeding the pot from 5 V gives better resolution on a 3.3 V ADC
options.explanation: The ADC can't measure above its reference, and on 3.3 V-only pins 5 V can damage the chip. It loses part of the range and risks damage.

questions.workedExample:
1. End pins: the divider is symmetric, so swapping reverses direction only.
2. Wiper to a rail: at full rotation one end-to-wiper segment is ~0 Ω. With that end at ground and the wiper on 3.3 V, the supply is shorted.
3. Documented supply: do not assume a VREF output can power a pot. If the ADC measures 0 to 3.3 V, the pot should span 0 to 3.3 V. Teensy 4.1's documentation (PJRC, checked 16 Oct 2026) says its analogue range is fixed at 0 to 3.3 V and the pins aren't 5 V tolerant. Check your own board.
4. 5 V feed: the wiper passes 3.3 V when it is 3.3 ÷ 5 = 66% of the way up an ideal linear pot from ground. Over the last third of the rotation the pin would see more than 3.3 V, outside its rating.

lessons.title: Linear and audio potentiometer tapers
lessons.summary: Taper describes resistance versus rotation.
lessons.body:
Taper describes resistance versus rotation.

## Linear and logarithmic (audio) taper
The **potentiometer taper** (or law) is how resistance changes with rotation.

- **Linear taper:** halfway round, the wiper is at half the total resistance. Output voltage is proportional to angle.
- **Logarithmic or "audio" taper:** the resistance changes slowly at first, then quickly. A common specification is a 10% log taper, meaning the wiper is at 10% of the total at mid-rotation. Hearing is roughly logarithmic, so a log pot makes an analogue volume control feel even.

| Rotation | Linear | 10% log (approx.) |
|---|---|---|
| 0% | 0% | 0% |
| 50% | 50% | 10% |
| 100% | 100% | 100% |

Two practical warnings:

- **Markings aren't standardised.** For example, Bourns PDB181-GTR uses its A-series audio curves and B0 linear curve. Other manufacturers and legacy parts use different letter schemes. Read the datasheet.
- **Cheap log pots are approximations,** often two linear segments joined near the middle.

> [!tip] For digital synths, usually choose linear
> When a pot feeds an ADC, you can apply any curve you like in software. A linear pot gives even resolution across the whole rotation, and code can map it to a logarithmic volume or exponential frequency response. A log pot is mostly useful when it directly controls an analogue audio level.

## Key takeaways

- Taper describes resistance versus rotation.
- Verify the manufacturer’s marking scheme rather than assuming a letter code.

## Further reading

- [Bourns PDB181-GTR: circuit and taper charts](https://www.bourns.com/docs/product-datasheets/PDB181-GTR.pdf)

questions.prompt: A pot marked "B10K" arrives from a supplier. What can you safely conclude?

options.text: It is 10 kΩ and certainly linear
options.explanation: "B" commonly means linear on Asian and US parts, but the letters aren't standardised. Some European makers use other letter schemes.

options.text: It is 10 kΩ log, because B stands for "bass"
options.explanation: There's no such convention. Taper codes vary by maker; "B" is often linear.

options.text: It is 10 kΩ, and the taper letter suggests linear on many parts but should be confirmed in the datasheet or by measuring
options.explanation: Correct. 10K is the track resistance. The taper letter convention varies between manufacturers, so check the datasheet, or measure the wiper resistance at mid-rotation (about 5 kΩ for linear, about 1 kΩ for a 10% log).

options.text: It is a 10 kΩ fixed resistor
options.explanation: "K" is the kilohm multiplier. The letter in front is the taper code of a potentiometer.

questions.workedExample:
1. "10K" gives the end-to-end track resistance: 10 kΩ.
2. The taper letter isn't standardised. A/B/C have different meanings between regions and makers.
3. Confirm: set the knob to mid-rotation and measure from one end to the wiper, with the pot out of circuit (unpowered).
   - About 5 kΩ means linear.
   - About 1 kΩ (or 9 kΩ from the other end) means a 10% log taper.

link.title: Bourns PDB181-GTR: circuit and taper charts

questions.prompt: Which of these are reasons to choose a *linear* pot for a knob read by a microcontroller ADC? Select all that apply.

options.text: You can apply any response curve in software after reading it
options.explanation: Correct. Code can map the reading to an exponential frequency or logarithmic level curve.

options.text: It spreads the ADC's resolution evenly across the rotation
options.explanation: Correct. With a log pot, much of the rotation is squeezed into a small part of the ADC range, wasting codes at one end.

options.text: Log pots can't be connected to ADCs
options.explanation: A log pot works electrically. It's just a divider with a track whose resistance share is not proportional to rotation. The point is that it's usually unnecessary.

options.text: Linear pots have lower noise than log pots in all cases
options.explanation: There's no general rule that taper decides noise. This isn't a reason taught in the lesson.

questions.workedExample:
1. The ADC converts voltage to a number. Any curve after that is arithmetic.
2. Linear pot: equal rotation gives equal ADC codes, so resolution is even everywhere.
3. 10% log pot: the first half of the rotation covers only 10% of the voltage range, so it gets about a tenth of the codes. That's coarse at the start.
4. Log pots are still useful when the pot directly sets an analogue audio level with no software in between.

lessons.title: Reading resistor colour bands
lessons.summary: Read digits, multiplier and tolerance separately.
lessons.body:
A synth build uses a small set of passive parts over and over. Each one has a **value** (what it does) and **ratings** (what it survives). Ignoring ratings or component polarity can damage parts even when the nominal value is correct.

### Reading the value
Through-hole resistors use colour bands defined by IEC 60062. Read from the end where the bands bunch together. The gold or silver tolerance band is usually at the other end, often slightly separated.

| Colour | Digit | Multiplier |
|---|---|---|
| Black | 0 | ×1 |
| Brown | 1 | ×10 |
| Red | 2 | ×100 |
| Orange | 3 | ×1k |
| Yellow | 4 | ×10k |
| Green | 5 | ×100k |
| Blue | 6 | ×1M |
| Violet | 7 | ×10M |
| Grey | 8 | ×100M |
| White | 9 | ×1G |
| Gold | | ×0.1 |
| Silver | | ×0.01 |

- **Four-band resistor code:** digit, digit, multiplier, tolerance. Yellow-violet-red-gold = 4, 7, ×100 = 4.7 kΩ ±5%.
- **Five-band resistor code** (precision): digit, digit, digit, multiplier, tolerance. Brown-black-black-red-brown = 1, 0, 0, ×100 = 10 kΩ ±1%.
- **Tolerance band:** brown ±1%, red ±2%, gold ±5%, silver ±10%.

The digit bands form a whole number, and the multiplier band scales it:

```formula
R = (10 × d_1 + d_2) × m
R = (10 × 4 + 7) × 100 Ω = 4700 Ω
where
R: the resistor's nominal value, in ohms (Ω)
d_1: the first digit band's number (yellow = 4)
d_2: the second digit band's number (violet = 7)
m: the multiplier band’s resistance scale, in ohms (Ω); red means 100 Ω per digit count
Ω: ohms, the unit of resistance
In words: read the digit bands as a two-digit number, then multiply by the multiplier band. Yellow-violet-red gives 47 × 100 = 4700 Ω = 4.7 kΩ.
```

A five-band resistor uses three significant digits. Brown-black-black-red-brown has three digits followed by the red multiplier and brown tolerance:

```formula
R = (100d_1 + 10d_2 + d_3)m
R = (100 × 1 + 10 × 0 + 0) × 100 Ω
R = 10,000 Ω = 10 kΩ
where
R: nominal resistance, in ohms (Ω)
d_1: first significant digit, brown gives one
d_2: second significant digit, black gives zero
d_3: third significant digit, black gives zero
m: resistance scale from the multiplier band, in ohms; red gives 100 Ω per digit count
Ω: ohms, the unit of resistance
kΩ: kilohms, one thousand ohms
In words: read the first three bands as one hundred, then apply the red scale of one hundred ohms. The brown tolerance band permits 1% initial variation.
```

Colours are easy to misread under poor light. Brown, red and orange look alike, and so do violet and grey. **Measure with a multimeter before fitting** (out of circuit) whenever you're unsure.

## Key takeaways

- Read digits, multiplier and tolerance separately.
- Confirm uncertain colours by measuring the unpowered resistor out of circuit.

## Further reading

- [Vishay: resistor colour code](https://www.vishay.com/docs/49411/resistor_color_code_calculator.pdf)

questions.prompt: A four-band resistor reads yellow, violet, orange, gold. What is it?

options.explanation: That would need a red (×100) multiplier. Orange is ×1000.
Correct. Yellow is 4 and violet is 7, giving 47. Orange multiplies by 1000, so 47 × 1000 = 47 kΩ. Gold means ±5%.
On a four-band resistor the third band is the multiplier, not a third digit.
Gold is ±5%. Silver is ±10%.

questions.workedExample:
1. Start from the end where the bands bunch up; the gold band is at the far end.
2. Read the bands and apply the four-band rule:

```formula
R = (10 × d_1 + d_2) × m
R = (10 × 4 + 7) × 1000 Ω
R = 47,000 Ω = 47 kΩ
where
R: the nominal resistance, in ohms (Ω)
d_1: band 1's digit (yellow = 4)
d_2: band 2's digit (violet = 7)
m: band 3’s resistance scale, in ohms; orange gives 1000 Ω per digit count
Ω: ohms, the unit of resistance
kΩ: kilohms; 1 kΩ = 1000 Ω
In words: the first two bands make 47, and the orange multiplier turns that into 47,000 Ω.
```

3. Gold indicates a 5% tolerance. For the nominal 47 kΩ part, that permits 44.65 kΩ to 49.35 kΩ.
4. If you're unsure of the colours, measure it out of circuit.

lessons.title: Preferred resistor values and ratings
lessons.summary: Choose an actual preferred value, then recalculate the result.
lessons.body:
Choose an actual preferred value, then recalculate the result.

### Preferred values
Resistors come in E-series values. E12 (for ±10%) has 12 values per decade (each tenfold range, such as 10 to 100): 10, 12, 15, 18, 22, 27, 33, 39, 47, 56, 68, 82. E24 adds more in between. You calculate an ideal value, then choose the nearest standard value in the safe direction.

The values aren't arbitrary. The underlying ideal sequence uses a constant ratio, so neighbours are approximately evenly spaced in percentage terms. The actual preferred values use a standard table:

```formula
v_n ≈ 10 × 10^{n/12}
v_4 ≈ 10 × 10^{4/12} ≈ 21.5 → 22
where
v_n: the n-th E12 value in the 10 to 100 decade (scale by 10, 100, 1000 … for other decades)
v_4: the value at step 4
n: the step number, 0 to 11 for the twelve values
10^{n/12}: ten raised to the power n ÷ 12; each step multiplies by about 1.21
≈: approximately equal to (the standard rounds each value to two digits)
→: rounds to
In words: each E12 value is about 21% above the one before, so neighbouring tolerance ranges are intended to sit close together. The actual rounded E12 table can leave small gaps; it is not an exact coverage proof. The rounded ideal sequence does not reproduce the whole E12 table. For example, the ideal positions near 27, 33, 39 and 47 give about 26.1, 31.6, 38.3 and 46.4. Use the published preferred-value table rather than generating production values from this approximation.
```

E24 uses the same idea with 24 steps per decade (n ÷ 24), each about 10% apart.

### Tolerance and resistor dissipation rating
- **Component tolerance**: how far a real part may be from its marked value. A 10 kΩ ±5% part may be anywhere from 9.5 to 10.5 kΩ. For a divider that sets a precise level, use 1% parts.
- **Resistor dissipation rating:** the most power the part can turn into heat continuously. Common small through-hole resistors are rated around 0.25 W. Check the datasheet. Calculate the power and leave margin. Running at half the rating or less is a common conservative practice.

```formula
R_min = R_nom(1 − t)
R_max = R_nom(1 + t)
R_min = 10 kΩ × 0.95 = 9.5 kΩ
R_max = 10 kΩ × 1.05 = 10.5 kΩ
where
R_nom: the nominal (marked) resistance, here 10 kΩ
t: the tolerance as a fraction, here ±5% = 0.05
R_min: the lowest value the part may really have
R_max: the highest value the part may really have
kΩ: kilohms; 1 kΩ = 1000 ohms (Ω)
In words: a ±5% part can be up to 5% below or above its marked value.
```

For the power check, use the resistor form of the power law from the voltage and current units:

```formula
P = I^2 R
P = (0.010 A)^2 × 330 Ω = 0.033 W
where
P: the power the resistor turns into heat, in watts (W)
I: the current through it, here 10 mA = 0.010 amperes (A)
I^2: the current squared
R: the resistance, here 330 ohms (Ω)
A: amperes, the unit of current
Ω: ohms, the unit of resistance
W: watts, the unit of power
In words: 10 mA through 330 Ω makes 33 mW of heat, about an eighth of a 0.25 W rating, so a small resistor is comfortable.
```

## Key takeaways

- Choose an actual preferred value, then recalculate the result.
- Tolerance, temperature and power derating belong in the design check.

## Further reading

- [Vishay: preferred-value table, IEC 60063](https://www.vishay.com/docs/28372/e-series.pdf)
- [Vishay: resistor colour code](https://www.vishay.com/docs/49411/resistor_color_code_calculator.pdf)
- [OpenStax: electrical energy and power](https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-2/pages/9-5-electrical-energy-and-power)

questions.prompt: You calculate a resistor value for an LED, then select a nearby preferred value. What should you check next?

options.text: Use the nominal calculation unchanged
options.explanation: The actual chosen value changes current, and tolerances change the worst case.

options.text: Recalculate current and heat using the chosen value and check tolerance and derating
options.explanation: Correct. The preferred value is a real part with limits; confirm both its function and its ratings.

options.text: Ignore the resistor dissipation rating if the supply is below 5 V
options.explanation: Low voltage can still produce enough current to overheat a resistor.

options.text: Choose a smaller resistor to make the LED safest
options.explanation: A smaller series resistance increases current for the same voltage difference.

questions.workedExample: Choose the next safe preferred value, then recompute the nominal current. For a hardware guarantee, check the highest supply voltage, lowest LED forward voltage and lowest resistor value allowed by tolerance. Finally compare resistor heat with the manufacturer’s derating curve at the actual ambient temperature.

lessons.title: Capacitor charging and RC time
lessons.summary: More capacitance slows voltage change for the same current.
lessons.body:
More capacitance slows voltage change for the same current.

A capacitor stores charge between conductors separated by an insulating dielectric. Capacitance is measured in farads; practical parts span picofarads to thousands of microfarads. The following model assumes ideal capacitance and a fixed charging current where a finite voltage-change per unit time is calculated.

### Behaviour
- An ideal capacitor **blocks steady DC current** once charged; a steady voltage can remain across it. Real capacitors have leakage and other losses.
- It **passes changes**, since current flows while its voltage is changing. This is why it can remove a DC offset from an audio signal or short fast noise to ground.
- Its voltage **can't jump instantly**. It changes at a rate set by the current:

```formula
ΔV / Δt = I / C
ΔV / Δt = 0.001 A / 0.000001 F
ΔV / Δt = 1000 V/s = 1 V/ms
where
ΔV: the change in the capacitor's voltage, in volts (V)
Δt: the time over which that change happens, in seconds (s)
Δ: delta, "the change in"
I: the current flowing into the capacitor, in amperes (A)
C: the capacitance, in farads (F)
A: amperes, the unit of current
F: farads, the unit of capacitance
V/s: volts per second
V/ms: volts per millisecond; 1 ms = 0.001 s
In words: the voltage rises faster with more current and slower with a bigger capacitor. 1 mA into 1 µF raises it by 1 V every millisecond. An instant jump would need infinite current, which is why it can't happen.
```

### The RC time constant
For an initially discharged ideal capacitor charged through a fixed resistor by a DC voltage step, the charging curve is exponential: fast at first, then slower and slower as it nears the supply. The **RC time constant** sets how long that takes:

```formula
τ = RC
τ = 10,000 Ω × 0.0000001 F = 0.001 s
where
τ: tau, the time constant, in seconds (s)
R: the resistance the capacitor charges through, here 10 kΩ = 10,000 ohms (Ω)
C: the capacitance, here 100 nF = 0.0000001 farads (F)
Ω: ohms, the unit of resistance
F: farads, the unit of capacitance
s: seconds; ohms × farads comes out in seconds
In words: a 10 kΩ resistor charging a 100 nF capacitor has a time constant of 1 millisecond. A bigger resistor or a bigger capacitor makes it slower.
```

The time constant is the unit of time for the charging curve:

```formula
V_C(t) = V_final(1 − e^{−t/τ})
V_C(τ) = V_final(1 − e^{−1})
V_C(τ) ≈ V_final × 0.632
where
V_C(t): the capacitor's voltage at time t, in volts (V)
t: the time since charging started, in seconds (s)
V_final: the voltage it is charging towards, in volts
e: Euler's number, about 2.718, the base of natural exponential growth and decay
e^{−t/τ}: e raised to the power minus t ÷ τ; it starts at 1 and falls towards 0
τ: tau, the time constant R × C, in seconds
≈: approximately equal to
In words: after one time constant the capacitor has covered about 63.2% of the way to its final voltage. Each further time constant covers 63.2% of what is left.
```

After five time constants it's within 1% of the final voltage (99.3%). The curve assumes an ideal capacitor and a steady source. When the source is removed and it discharges through a resistor, the remaining capacitor voltage decays exponentially, approaching 0 V.

```python
import math

tau = 10e3 * 100e-9    # 10 kΩ, 100 nF
for n in (1, 2, 3, 5):
    # Charge after n time constants.
    pct = 100 * (1 - math.exp(-n))
    ms = n * tau * 1e3
    t = f"{n} tau = {ms:.1f} ms"
    print(f"{t}: {pct:.1f}%")
```

```
1 tau = 1.0 ms: 63.2%
2 tau = 2.0 ms: 86.5%
3 tau = 3.0 ms: 95.0%
5 tau = 5.0 ms: 99.3%
```

## Key takeaways

- More capacitance slows voltage change for the same current.
- An ideal RC step reaches about 63.2% after one time constant.

## Further reading

- [OpenStax: ideal RC circuits](https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-2/pages/10-5-rc-circuits)

lessons.title: The RC low-pass cutoff
lessons.summary: An unloaded RC low-pass has its cutoff at one over two pi times RC.
lessons.body:
An unloaded RC low-pass has its cutoff at one over two pi times RC.

## An RC low-pass filter

RC circuits show up across synth hardware. They smooth a noisy knob and slow a bouncing switch. A resistor followed by a capacitor to ground is also the simplest low-pass filter (an RC low-pass filter): it passes slow changes and shorts fast ones to ground. Its cut-off frequency is:

```formula
f_c = 1 / (2πRC)
f_c = 1 / (2π × 10,000 Ω × 100 nF)
f_c ≈ 159 Hz
where
f_c: the cut-off frequency, in hertz (Hz): where the output has fallen to about 71% of the input (−3 dB)
π: pi, about 3.14159
R: the resistance, here 10 kΩ = 10,000 ohms (Ω)
C: the capacitance, here 100 nF = 0.0000001 farads (F)
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
Ω: ohms, the unit of resistance
nF: nanofarads; one billionth of a farad
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: the same 10 kΩ and 100 nF that give a 1 ms time constant start cutting frequencies above about 159 Hz. Bigger R or C gives a lower cut-off.
```

This assumes whatever reads the capacitor draws almost no current. A load across the capacitor changes the cut-off, just as it loads a divider.

## Key takeaways

- An unloaded RC low-pass has its cutoff at one over two pi times RC.
- Loading and nonideal components change the simple model.

## Further reading

- [TI Precision Labs: passive RC response](https://www.ti.com.cn/content/dam/videos/external-videos/zh-cn/4/3816841626001/6119035031001.mp4/subassets/passive_components_and_circuits_2.pdf)

- [OpenStax: ideal RC circuits](https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-2/pages/10-5-rc-circuits)

```formula
where
```
