options.text: The rails are split
options.explanation: Split rails would show open circuit along the rail, not a brief beep across + and −.

options.text: Normal: the meter's test current is charging the circuit's capacitors, then the reading settles high
options.explanation: Correct. Decoupling and bulk capacitors look like a short for a moment and then like an open circuit once charged.

questions.workedExample:
1. Unpowered, the meter applies a small test voltage.
2. Discharged capacitors draw current at first, so the reading starts low and may beep.
3. As they charge, the current falls and the reading rises towards the circuit's true resistance.
4. A real short gives a steady, very low reading. Stop and find it before applying power.

questions.prompt: You have a bench supply with an adjustable current limit. Your prototype should draw about 40 mA. How should you set it for first power-up, and why?

options.text: Maximum, so the circuit never starves
options.explanation: With the limit at maximum, a short draws all the supply can give, which can damage parts or wiring.

options.text: Use a documented initial limit modestly above expected draw, perhaps 60–80 mA for this illustrative circuit, and check startup and component limits
options.explanation: Correct. Limiting sustained fault current can help reveal a problem, but the supply’s current-limit reaction delay and stored energy mean it cannot guarantee that every component survives a short.

options.text: Exactly 40 mA
options.explanation: Startup surges and normal variation could trip the limit and confuse you. Leave some headroom.

options.text: The current limit doesn't matter at low voltage
options.explanation: Low voltage limits shock risk, but a short at low voltage can still pass enough current to overheat parts and wiring.

questions.workedExample:
1. Estimate the normal draw: 40 mA.
2. Set the limit with headroom for inrush and variation, perhaps 1.5–2×.
3. Power up and watch the supply's current reading and limit indicator.
4. If it hits the limit, the voltage collapses instead of the current rising. Switch off and find the fault.
5. Once the circuit is verified, raise the limit to suit the real load.

The 60–80 mA range is an illustrative starting point, not a universal safe limit. Check inrush, supply output capacitance and the smallest allowed current or energy in the real circuit.

questions.prompt: Which of these belong in the pre-power checklist? Select all that apply.

options.text: Measure resistance across a component while the circuit is powered, to confirm its value
options.explanation: Resistance must be measured unpowered. Powered, the reading is wrong and the meter can be damaged.

options.text: Check every polarised part's orientation against the schematic
options.explanation: Correct. Reversed electrolytics, diodes and ICs are among the commonest fatal mistakes.

options.text: Measure resistance between the supply rails with power off
options.explanation: Correct. It finds dead shorts before any current flows.

options.text: Measure the supply's output voltage on its own before connecting it
options.explanation: Correct. It confirms you're about to apply the voltage you think you are.

questions.workedExample:
Pre-power checklist:

1. Visual: component polarity, stray leads.
2. Unpowered: resistance or continuity across the rails. Steady near zero means a short.
3. Supply: measure its voltage before connecting.
4. Current limit set, if available.
5. Power up, watch for heat or smell, then measure rails at the chips.

Resistance measurements are always made with the power off. The measurement units explain why.

lessons.title: Voltage measurement, ranges and meter loading
lessons.summary: Voltage is measured across two points with the correct jack and range.
lessons.body:
Measuring tells you whether the circuit is doing what you calculated. Soldering makes a circuit permanent. Both are hands-on skills with a few rules that, if you ignore them, destroy fuses, parts or your lungs.

> [!warning] Low-voltage work only
> Everything here assumes low-voltage DC circuits powered from USB, batteries or a bench supply. Don't use these techniques on mains-powered equipment. Mains measurement needs suitably rated (CAT-rated) instruments and training, and it's outside this project's scope.


A digital multimeter (DMM) has a rotary switch and usually three or four input jacks:

- **COM:** the common (black) lead. It stays here for everything.
- **VΩ** (shared with current only on some meters): red lead for voltage, resistance, continuity and diode test.
- **mA / µA:** red lead for small currents, protected by a fuse.
- **A or 10A:** red lead for large currents, fused only if the meter’s manual specifies it; some inexpensive meters leave that input unfused.

The jack layout differs between meters, so read the manual.


### Voltage: in parallel
Put the probes **across** the thing you're measuring, black on the reference (usually ground) and red on the point of interest. Nothing gets disconnected.

```diagram
  +5V ──[ R1 ]──┬──[ LED ]── GND
                │
             red probe
   (black probe on GND)
```

- Use **DC volts** (V⎓) for supply rails and logic. AC volts usually rejects the DC component, so it will not tell you a rail’s steady voltage. An average-responding meter is RMS-calibrated for a sine wave; other waveforms need a suitable true-RMS instrument within its frequency, crest-factor and range limits.
- A digital meter's voltage input is high-impedance, typically around 10 MΩ on DC volts, though some meters and ranges differ (check your meter's specification). It barely loads most circuits, but on a very high-resistance divider the meter itself pulls the reading down. Lesson 2's loading rule applies to meters too.
- A negative DC reading means the red probe is below the black probe in voltage. The probes may be reversed, or the measured voltage may genuinely have the opposite polarity.

### Choosing ranges
Autoranging meters choose for you. On a manual meter:

- **Start on a range above the largest value you expect,** then step down for resolution.
- An "OL" or "1" display means meter over-range. Go up a range.
- For current, start on the highest range if you're unsure, which on many meters means moving the red lead to the A jack.

## Key takeaways

- Voltage is measured across two points with the correct jack and range.
- The meter’s finite input impedance can load high-resistance circuits.

## Further reading

- [SparkFun: using a multimeter](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/how-to-use-a-multimeter/all)
- [SparkFun: voltage dividers](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/voltage-dividers/all)

questions.prompt: How do you connect a multimeter to measure the voltage on an LED's anode?

options.text: In series: break the wire to the anode and connect the meter across the gap
options.explanation: That's how you measure current. Voltage is measured across two points without breaking anything.

options.text: In parallel: black probe on ground, red probe on the anode, meter set to DC volts
options.explanation: Correct. A voltage is a difference between two points, so the probes go across them. Nothing is disconnected.

options.text: In parallel, with the red lead in the mA jack
options.explanation: In the mA jack the meter is nearly a short. Connected across a voltage it shorts the circuit and blows the fuse.

options.text: Either way, as long as the meter is on autorange
options.explanation: Autorange picks the scale, not the connection method. Voltage is always measured in parallel.

questions.workedExample:
1. Voltage is between two points: here, anode and ground.
2. Red lead in VΩ, black in COM, switch to DC volts.
3. Black probe to ground, red probe to the anode.
4. Read. A negative sign means the probes are swapped.

questions.prompt: A divider of two 10 MΩ resistors across 3.3 V should give 1.65 V. Your DMM, with a 10 MΩ input impedance, reads about 1.1 V. Why?

options.text: The meter's 10 MΩ input is in parallel with the bottom 10 MΩ, making it 5 MΩ, so the divider gives 3.3 V × 5/15 = 1.1 V
options.explanation: Correct. A meter is a load like any other. Here it's as large as the divider's own resistors.

options.text: The meter is broken
options.explanation: The meter is behaving correctly. It's loading the circuit.

options.text: Voltage must be measured in series
options.explanation: Voltage is measured in parallel. The issue is the meter's finite input resistance.

options.text: 10 MΩ resistors are too noisy to measure
options.explanation: Noise isn't the cause of a steady, predictable 1.1 V reading.

questions.workedExample:
1. The meter's input resistance (10 MΩ here) appears in parallel with whatever it measures, so it becomes part of the divider:

```formula
R2_eff = R2 ∥ R_meter
R2_eff = 10 MΩ ∥ 10 MΩ = 5 MΩ
Vout = Vin R2_eff / (R1 + R2_eff)
Vout = 3.3 V × 5 / (10 + 5) = 1.1 V
where
R2_eff: the bottom resistor with the meter in parallel, in megohms (MΩ)
R2: the bottom resistor, here 10 MΩ
R_meter: the meter's input resistance, here 10 MΩ
∥: "in parallel with": (a × b) / (a + b)
Vout: the voltage the meter actually reads, in volts (V)
Vin: the supply, here 3.3 V
R1: the top resistor, here 10 MΩ
MΩ: megohms; 1 MΩ = 1,000,000 ohms
V: volts
In words: the meter halves the bottom resistor, so the divider gives a third of 3.3 V instead of half.
```

2. On low-impedance circuits (kilohms) the effect is negligible. On megohm circuits, account for it or use a buffered measurement.

questions.prompt: On a manual-ranging meter, you need to measure a voltage you expect to be about 3.3 V. The ranges are 200 mV, 2 V, 20 V and 200 V. Which do you choose?

options.text: 200 mV, for the most precision
options.explanation: 3.3 V is far above 200 mV, so the meter shows meter over-range (OL or 1).

options.text: 2 V
options.explanation: 3.3 V exceeds 2 V range limit, so it shows meter over-range.
Correct. It's the lowest range above the anticipated reading, giving the best resolution without meter over-range.

options.text: 200 V, to be safe
options.explanation: It works but wastes resolution: you'd see 3 V or 3.3 V rather than 3.30 V.

questions.workedExample:
1. Choose the lowest range that's still above the anticipated reading.
2. 3.3 V > 2 V, so 2 V and 200 mV meter over-range.
3. 20 V gives readings like 3.30 V.
4. If you don't know the value at all, start at the highest range and step down.

lessons.title: Measuring series current and burden voltage
lessons.summary: Power off before inserting the meter in series.
lessons.body:
Power off before inserting the meter in series.

### Current: in series
To measure current, the current has to flow **through** the meter. Break the circuit and insert the meter into the gap:

```diagram
  +5V ──[ R1 ]──  ✂  ──[ LED ]── GND
              red    black
               └─ meter ─┘
```

1. Power off.
2. Move the red lead to the **mA** jack (or the A jack for larger currents) and select the current range.
3. Open the circuit at one point and connect the meter across the gap.
4. Power on and read.
5. **Power off and move the red lead back to VΩ** before your next measurement.

> [!warning] The classic fuse-blower
> In current mode the meter is almost a short circuit, by design. Put it *across* a supply (as you would for voltage) and you short the supply through the meter. The meter's fuse is there to blow in that case. Replace it only with the **exact type and rating** the manual specifies. Forgetting to move the red lead back to VΩ is the commonest way to do this.

Meters also have a **burden voltage**: the small voltage the meter drops while measuring current. It comes from the series resistance of the shunt and other current-path parts, including the fuse and connections. Model their combined resistance to estimate it with Ohm’s law:

```formula
V_burden = I × R_shunt
V_burden = 0.010 A × 10 Ω = 0.1 V
where
V_burden: the voltage lost across the meter, in volts (V)
I: the current being measured, here 10 mA = 0.010 amperes (A)
R_shunt: the combined series resistance of the meter’s current path on that range, in ohms (Ω); 10 Ω is illustrative, so check the specified burden voltage and lead effects
V: volts
A: amperes
Ω: ohms
In words: the meter steals a little voltage from the circuit, more at higher currents and on more sensitive ranges.
```

On sensitive low-voltage circuits that stolen voltage can slightly change what you're measuring. Compare that drop with the voltage left for the current-setting parts and with your allowed error. Even in a 5 V circuit, a 0.1 V drop can matter if an LED leaves little resistor headroom.

## Key takeaways

- Power off before inserting the meter in series.
- Restore the voltage jack after current measurements.

## Further reading

- [Fluke: current measurement](https://www.fluke.com/en-gb/learn/blog/digital-multimeters/how-to-measure-current)
- [SparkFun: using a multimeter](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/how-to-use-a-multimeter/all)

questions.prompt: You've just measured an LED's current with the red lead in the mA jack. Without changing anything, you touch the probes across the 5 V supply rails to check the voltage. What happens?

options.text: You read 5 V
options.explanation: In current mode the meter's input is a low-resistance shunt, not a voltmeter.

options.text: You read 0 V and nothing else happens
options.explanation: The display may read near zero, but a large current flows through the shunt, which usually blows the fuse.

options.text: You short the supply through the meter's low-resistance current shunt, which typically blows the meter's fuse
options.explanation: Correct. Current mode is nearly a short circuit by design. Always move the red lead back to VΩ after measuring current.

options.text: The meter switches to voltage mode automatically
options.explanation: Most meters don't detect this. A few warn if the lead is in the wrong jack, but you can't rely on it.

questions.workedExample:
1. In current mode, current enters the mA jack, flows through a small shunt resistor, and leaves via COM.
2. Placed across the rails, the meter connects + to − through that shunt.
3. The current is limited only by the supply and the shunt, and a correctly fused current input may blow its fuse. A current-limited supply might limit first; an unfused input can be damaged. Never try this.
4. Habit: power off, move the lead back to VΩ, and switch back to volts every time.

questions.prompt: You want to know how much current your breadboard prototype draws from its 5 V supply. Where should the meter go?

options.text: Across the 5 V and GND rails
options.explanation: That's a voltage measurement, and in current mode it shorts the supply.

options.text: Across one resistor in the circuit
options.explanation: In current mode this shorts that resistor. In voltage mode it gives the resistor's voltage, which tells you only that branch's current via Ohm's law.

options.text: Between ground and the meter's case
options.explanation: That's not a measurement path at all.

options.text: In series in the supply's positive lead: disconnect the + wire and route it through the meter
options.explanation: Correct. All the prototype's current then flows through the meter.

questions.workedExample:
1. Power off before opening the supply lead. Current must flow *through* the meter to be measured.
2. Total supply current flows in the supply's + lead, so break that lead.
3. Choose the current jack and range rated above the expected draw (use the A jack if the mA limit could be exceeded), connect the meter between supply + and the breadboard's + rail.
4. Power up and read, then power off, restore the wire, and move the red lead back to VΩ.

lessons.title: Unpowered resistance and continuity checks
lessons.summary: Remove all power and discharge capacitors before resistance tests.
lessons.body:
Remove all power and discharge capacitors before resistance tests.

### Resistance and continuity: only unpowered
Resistance mode works by passing a small test current from the meter's own battery and measuring the resulting voltage. So:

- **The circuit must be unpowered.** External voltages corrupt the reading and can damage the meter.
- **Measure parts out of circuit, or lift one leg.** In circuit, other paths in parallel lower the reading. Lesson 2's parallel rule explains why.
- **Continuity mode** beeps below a low resistance threshold. Use it to check wires, solder joints, breadboard rails and switch contacts, and to find shorts.
- **Diode test mode** shows a diode's forward voltage (about 0.5–0.7 V for silicon) one way and open circuit the other. It often lights an LED faintly too, which is handy for identifying LED orientation.
- Discharge large capacitors before measuring around them.

## Key takeaways

- Remove all power and discharge capacitors before resistance tests.
- Parallel circuit paths can invalidate an in-circuit component measurement.

## Further reading

- [Fluke: resistance measurement](https://www.fluke.com/en-us/learn/blog/digital-multimeters/how-to-measure-resistance)
- [SparkFun: using a multimeter](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/how-to-use-a-multimeter/all)

questions.prompt: Why must resistance and continuity be measured with the circuit unpowered?

options.text: The meter supplies its own small test current and measures the resulting voltage. An external voltage corrupts the reading and can damage the meter
options.explanation: Correct. Resistance mode relies on the meter's own known source, so any other source interferes.

options.text: Powered circuits have no resistance
options.explanation: Resistance exists whether or not a circuit is powered. The problem is the measurement method.

options.text: To save the meter's battery
options.explanation: Battery life isn't the reason. Accuracy and meter safety are.

options.text: It doesn't matter for resistance, only for continuity
options.explanation: Both modes use the same principle and both need an unpowered circuit.

questions.workedExample:
1. In Ω mode the meter pushes a small known current through the part and measures the voltage that results:

```formula
R = V / I
R = 0.1 V / 0.0001 A = 1000 Ω
where
R: the resistance the meter displays, in ohms (Ω)
V: the voltage the meter measures across the part, in volts (V)
I: the known test current the meter supplies, in amperes (A); 0.1 mA here is only an illustration
A: amperes
Ω: ohms
In words: the meter works out resistance from its own current and the voltage it sees, so the part must carry no other current.
```

2. If the circuit is powered, its own voltages add to or subtract from the meter's, so the result is meaningless.
3. Large enough voltages can damage the meter's input.
4. Also discharge capacitors, and measure parts out of circuit when other paths could run in parallel.

lessons.title: What an oscilloscope shows and its ground clip
lessons.summary: A scope shows waveform shape and timing, within its limits.
lessons.body:
A scope shows waveform shape and timing, within its limits.

## The oscilloscope: seeing voltage over time
A multimeter gives one number: a DC value or an AC summary whose meaning depends on the meter and waveform. An **oscilloscope** draws voltage against time, so you can see what's actually happening:

- the shape of an audio waveform, and whether it clips;
- noise and supply ripple riding on a rail;
- logic or PWM signals and their timing;
- switch bounce lasting a few milliseconds.

Core controls:

- **Vertical (V/div):** volts per grid square.
- **Horizontal (time/div):** seconds per grid square.
- **Trigger** (the oscilloscope trigger): the condition (a level and a rising or falling edge) that starts each sweep at the same point, so a repeating waveform stands still on screen.
- **Probe ×1/×10:** ×10 probes load the circuit less and extend bandwidth. Set the scope to match the probe.

> [!warning] Probe ground clips
> On a typical mains-powered bench scope, the probe's ground clip is connected to protective earth through the scope. In this low-voltage project, connect it only to the documented ground reference after checking the instrument and circuit grounding. Multiple ordinary channel ground clips are normally connected together. Connecting it to another point in a circuit that's also earth-referenced creates a short through the probe. A circuit is earth-referenced if anything connected to it ties its ground to earth: a desktop PC's USB port usually does, and so do some laptop adapters with three-pin plugs, while two-pin laptop adapters usually leave the output floating. Don't rely on knowing which. To measure across a component, use two correctly configured probes (both grounds on circuit ground) and the scope’s A − B maths, or a suitable differential probe. Keep each probe’s voltage, common-mode, bandwidth and instrument ratings within its specified limits; subtraction does not isolate an ordinary probe. Never defeat a scope's safety earth to "float" it. Instrument manuals strongly warn against it.

The project doesn't require owning a scope at first. A multimeter covers the foundation exercises. Consider a scope when you need to debug noise, audio clipping or timing that a meter can't show.

## Key takeaways

- A scope shows waveform shape and timing, within its limits.
- Keep ordinary probe ground clips on the documented circuit ground.

## Further reading

- [Tektronix: floating measurements and grounding](https://www.tek.com/en/documents/technical-brief/floating-oscilloscope-measurements-and-operator-protection)

questions.prompt: Your audio prototype is powered from a desktop PC's USB port. For this scenario, its USB ground is confirmed connected to protective earth. You connect a mains-powered bench scope and clip the probe's ground lead to the output of an op-amp stage to "measure across a resistor". The output dies. What happened?

options.text: The scope's input impedance loaded the op-amp
options.explanation: A ×10 probe is around 10 MΩ, which is far too light to kill an op-amp output.

options.text: The trigger setting was wrong
options.explanation: Trigger affects the display, not the circuit.

options.text: Scopes can't measure audio frequencies
options.explanation: General-purpose oscilloscopes commonly cover audio frequencies; check the actual instrument and probe specifications. Bandwidth does not explain a grounded clip shorting this output.

options.text: The probe's ground clip connects to protective earth. Through the PC's earthed USB ground, it shorted that op-amp output to ground
options.explanation: Correct. On a typical bench scope the ground clip is earthed. The PC also ties the circuit's ground to earth, so connecting the scope ground to any non-ground node shorts that node to circuit ground.

questions.workedExample:
1. Bench scopes typically tie every probe's ground clip to the mains protective earth.
2. The scenario confirms that this PC’s USB ground is earthed, so the circuit ground is earth-referenced too.
3. Connecting the probe ground to an op-amp output connects that output to earth, which is the circuit's ground: a short.
4. Laptops vary. Two-pin adapters usually leave the output floating, while some three-pin adapters earth it. Don't rely on knowing which: assume the circuit may be earth-referenced.
5. Rule: clip the ground only to circuit ground. Measure across a component with two probes (A − B maths) or a differential probe. Never defeat the scope's safety earth.

lessons.title: Solder alloys, fume controls and iron temperature
lessons.summary: Capture rosin flux fume at source and use appropriate eye and hand precautions.
lessons.body:
Capture rosin flux fume at source and use appropriate eye and hand precautions.

### Safety
- **Rosin flux fume:** the HSE states that rosin (colophony)-based solder flux fume is "a common cause of occupational asthma". Work in a well-ventilated space and use suitable local fume extraction that captures fume at the source. A desk fan merely moving fume around the room is not equivalent to extraction. Consider rosin-free or reduced-rosin fluxes.
- **Lead:** if you use leaded solder, wash your hands afterwards and don't eat or drink while soldering.
- **Eyes:** wear safety glasses. Flux can spit and clipped leads fly.
- **Burns:** always put the iron back in its stand. Never catch a falling iron. Keep the cable clear.
- **Unpowered:** never solder a circuit while it's powered.

### Leaded or lead-free
| | Leaded (63/37 Sn-Pb) | Lead-free (e.g. Sn-Ag-Cu) |
|---|---|---|
| Melting point | 183 °C (eutectic) | SAC305: 217–219 °C |
| Ease | Flows easily, forgiving | Needs more heat, less forgiving |
| Joint look | Shiny | Duller, slightly grainy |
| Health/regulation | Contains lead | Used to meet lead restrictions where RoHS applies; exemptions exist |

Use an alloy and flux suited to the component, board and applicable work requirements. Follow their manufacturer’s instructions; this is not a judgement that every hobby use has the same legal or health requirements. A eutectic alloy melts and solidifies at a single temperature, so it has no pasty phase where movement spoils the joint.

### Temperature
Use a **temperature-controlled iron**. SparkFun's through-hole soldering guide suggests a "good medium heat (325-375 degrees C)" as a starting point. Lead-free usually needs the upper end. If the solder smokes heavily or flux burns off instantly, turn the heat down. If the joint won't flow within a few seconds, a bigger tip often helps more than more heat.

## Key takeaways

- Capture rosin flux fume at source and use appropriate eye and hand precautions.
- Follow the alloy, tool and component instructions for temperature.

## Further reading

- [HSE INDG249: rosin flux fume controls](https://www.hse.gov.uk/pubns/indg249.pdf)
- [Kester: alloy temperature chart](https://www.kester.com/knowledge-base/alloy-temperature-chart)
- [Kester SAC305: technical data sheet, 16 March 2022](https://www.kester.com/DesktopModules/Bring2mind/DMX/API/Entries/Download?DownloadMethod=attachment&EntryId=45147&PortalId=0)
- [SparkFun: through-hole soldering](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/how-to-solder-through-hole-soldering/all)

lessons.title: Making and inspecting a through-hole joint
lessons.summary: Heat both pad and lead and hold the joint still while it solidifies.
lessons.body:
Heat both pad and lead and hold the joint still while it solidifies.

### Technique for a through-hole joint
1. **Clean and tin the tip:** wipe on a damp sponge or brass wool, then melt a little solder on the tip. This helps heat transfer.
2. **Heat both the pad and the lead together** with the side of the tip touching both.
3. **Feed solder into the joint,** not onto the iron. It should flow around the lead and across the pad. Flux in the solder's core cleans oxide so the solder can wet the metal.
4. **Remove the solder, then the iron.** A small joint takes a few seconds in total.
5. **Don't move the joint** until it solidifies.
6. Trim the lead above the joint.

### Inspecting a joint
```diagram
  good:   /‾\      concave cone, wets
         /   \     both pad and lead
  ──────/     \──────

  cold:  ( ● )     ball sitting on pad,
  ──────(     )──  dull, not wetted
```

- **Good:** a smooth, concave "volcano" fillet that wets both the pad and the lead. Shiny with leaded solder, somewhat duller with lead-free.
- **Cold joint:** dull, grainy or lumpy, often balled up. Either the pad or the lead wasn't hot enough. Reheat with a little fresh flux.
- **Bridge** (solder bridge): solder joining adjacent pads. Remove it with desoldering braid or by dragging a clean tip.
- **Insufficient:** the hole isn't filled or the pad isn't covered.
- **Overheated:** burnt flux, discoloured board, or a **lifted pad** (the copper peeling off). Use less time and the right tip.

With power disconnected and capacitors discharged, test the intended nets with **continuity mode** and look for bridges under a magnifier. A beep alone does not prove a mechanically reliable joint or distinguish an intended circuit path from a bridge.

## Key takeaways

- Heat both pad and lead and hold the joint still while it solidifies.
- Inspect wetting, shape, bridges and damage, not shine alone.

## Further reading

- [Adafruit: excellent soldering](https://learn.adafruit.com/adafruit-guide-excellent-soldering)
- [SparkFun: through-hole soldering](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/how-to-solder-through-hole-soldering/all)

lessons.title: Calculating an audio hum budget
lessons.summary: Small return-wire voltages can matter after amplification.
lessons.body:
A synth that works can still be unusable if it hums, buzzes or whines. Noise can come from components, interference, supply coupling and **how currents return**. These units focus on wiring, grounding and power coupling. This lesson gives you the mental model to diagnose noise in your own studio: a synth board, a Digitakt, an audio interface and a computer running Ableton.

> [!warning] Never touch the safety earth
> Some "fixes" for hum online involve removing or cutting the earth connection of mains equipment ("ground lifting" the plug). **Never do this.** The protective earth is what makes a fault safe. Rane's grounding note says: "Safety regulations require that all original grounding means provided from the factory be left intact for safe operation." Everything in this lesson works at the signal level or uses equipment designed for isolation.

## Why audio is so sensitive
Digital links have specified threshold margins, sometimes only a few tenths of a volt. Audio has no digital-style logic threshold: added noise can be amplified, but whether it is audible depends on gain, spectrum, masking and the listening system. A commonly used consumer nominal line reference is −10 dBV; actual device outputs and input headroom vary, so read the exact manuals. Converting that level to volts:

```formula
V = 1 V × 10^{L/20}
V = 1 V × 10^{−10/20} ≈ 0.316 V
where
V: the signal's RMS voltage, in volts (V)
L: the level in dBV, decibels relative to 1 volt RMS; here −10 dBV
10^{L/20}: ten raised to the power L ÷ 20, which turns decibels back into a voltage ratio
dBV: decibels relative to 1 V RMS
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: −10 dBV is about 0.316 volts RMS, roughly a third of a volt.
```

A clean system's noise sits tens of decibels below that, so a few hundred microvolts of hum can be clearly audible. To see how far below the signal some hum sits, find the hum voltage with Ohm's law, then express the ratio in decibels:

```formula
V_hum = I_loop R_shield
V_hum = 0.001 A × 0.1 Ω = 0.0001 V
L_SH = 20 log_10(V_sig / V_hum)
L_SH = 20 log_10(0.316 V / 0.0001 V)
L_SH ≈ 20 × 3.5 = 70 dB
where
V_hum: the hum RMS voltage added to the signal, in volts (V); 0.0001 V is 100 µV
I_loop: the RMS unwanted current flowing in the cable shield, here 1 mA = 0.001 amperes (A)
R_shield: the shield's resistance, here 100 mΩ = 0.1 ohms (Ω)
L_SH: the signal-to-hum ratio, in decibels (dB)
V_sig: the signal voltage, here 0.316 V RMS
log_10: the base-10 logarithm: the power you raise 10 to in order to get the number (log_10(1000) = 3)
V: volts
A: amperes
Ω: ohms
dB: decibels; 20 dB is a factor of 10 in voltage
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: 1 mA through a 0.1 Ω shield makes 100 µV of hum, which sits about 70 dB below a −10 dBV signal.
```

The same sums in Python:

```python
import math

def db(ratio):
    return 20 * math.log10(ratio)

i_loop = 0.001    # 1 mA of 50 Hz current
r_shield = 0.1    # 100 mΩ cable shield
# Illustrative RMS drop across the shield.
v_hum = i_loop * r_shield

v_sig = 10 ** (-10 / 20)  # -10 dBV line
print(f"hum: {v_hum * 1e6:.0f} uV")
print(f"signal: {v_sig:.3f} V")
print(f"S/hum: {db(v_sig / v_hum):.1f} dB")
```

```
hum: 100 uV
signal: 0.316 V
S/hum: 70.0 dB
```

The 1 mA and 100 mΩ figures are illustrative, not measured; real loop currents and shield resistances vary widely. The mechanism (loop current × shield resistance adds to the signal) is the one Wikipedia's ground-loop article derives. Hum only 70 dB below the signal may be heard in quiet passages or with gain applied afterwards.

## Key takeaways

- Small return-wire voltages can matter after amplification.
- State whether voltages are RMS before using a decibel ratio.

## Further reading

- [RaneNote 110: system interconnection](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/note110.html)
- [Analog Devices MT-031: converter grounding](https://www.analog.com/media/en/training-seminars/tutorials/MT-031.pdf)

options.explanation: This misplaces the voltage by several orders of magnitude. The hum is 100 µV, not 30 mV.

options.text: About 35 dB
options.explanation: This uses 10 × log₁₀ instead of 20 × log₁₀ (10 × 3.5 = 35). Voltage ratios in decibels use 20 × log₁₀.

options.explanation: This doubles the correct figure. Check the arithmetic: the voltage ratio is about 3162, its base-10 logarithm is about 3.5, and 20 × 3.5 = 70.

```formula
R: the shield resistance, here 100 mΩ = 0.1 ohms (Ω)

V_sig: the signal, −10 dBV ≈ 0.316 V RMS

dB: decibels; 20 dB per factor of 10 in voltage
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: the signal is about 3160 times the hum, and a voltage ratio of about 3160 is 70 dB.
```

2. 70 dB below the signal may be audible in quiet passages or after gain, which is why small loop currents matter.

lessons.title: Finding ground loops in a studio
lessons.summary: Map every ground path, including USB and audio.
lessons.body:
Map every ground path, including USB and audio.

## Ground loops
A **ground loop** forms when two pieces of equipment are connected to each other by more than one ground path. Typically:

1. each one's mains protective earth, through the wall wiring, and
2. the shield or sleeve of the audio cable between them.

```diagram
 Device A ──cable shield── Device B
    │                         │
  earth                     earth
    │                         │
    └────── mains wiring ─────┘
       (loop encloses an area)
```

Stray magnetic fields from mains wiring and transformers induce a current around this loop, and the two earth points may also sit at slightly different potentials. As Rane's note puts it, the hum appears "when this current flows through a unit's audio signal ground". In an **unbalanced connection** the cable's shield *is* the signal return, so the voltage drop along it adds straight to the audio.

The result is hum at the mains frequency (50 Hz in the UK) and its harmonics. A rectified-supply component at 100 Hz is also common.

### Ground loops with USB

Low-voltage gear can form loops too. A common case in a synth studio:

- The synth board is powered over USB from the computer.
- The computer connects to the audio interface over USB.
- The synth's audio output goes to the interface's input.

That's two ground paths between synth and interface: through the audio cable and through USB via the computer. Digital noise on the USB ground (from the computer's processor, display and charger) flows partly through the audio cable's shield. It's often heard as whine or buzzing that changes with computer activity.

### Diagnosing and fixing

Work from least invasive to most:

1. **Diagnose by elimination.** Disconnect cables one at a time and listen. Run the synth from a battery power bank to see whether the USB ground path is the culprit. Note whether the noise is a steady 50/100 Hz hum or a varying digital whine.
2. **Plug all mains equipment into the same outlet or power strip,** so the earth paths are short and close together. This is common studio practice.
3. **Use balanced connections** where both ends support them. Hum that appears equally on both conductors is rejected by a balanced input.
4. **Break the loop with a device made for it:** an audio isolation transformer (DI box or ground-loop isolator) in the audio line, or a USB isolator on the USB connection. Use only devices documented to suit the signal level, impedances, bandwidth and required isolation. A USB isolator must support the required USB speed and power arrangement; its data and power paths must actually break the unwanted ground route. An active DI box is not automatically transformer-isolated. Keep every protective earth intact.
5. **Design it out:** in your own build, give the synth one clear ground reference and avoid creating extra ground paths.

DIN MIDI is designed this way already: the receiving end uses an **opto-isolator**, so a MIDI cable doesn't join the grounds of the two devices. The MIDI module covers the circuit.

## Key takeaways

- Map every ground path, including USB and audio.
- Use documented signal isolation and preserve every protective earth.

## Further reading

- [RaneNote 110: system interconnection](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/note110.html)
- [Analog Devices MT-031: converter grounding](https://www.analog.com/media/en/training-seminars/tutorials/MT-031.pdf)

4. Then fix with balanced connections, isolation transformers or USB isolators.
5. Never alter mains earthing.

lessons.title: Shared return impedance and analogue grounding
lessons.summary: Separate noisy return currents from sensitive references.
lessons.body:
Separate noisy return currents from sensitive references.

## Shared impedance and star grounding
Ground loops are one mechanism. The other, inside your own circuit, is **shared-impedance coupling**. Every ground wire or track has resistance (and inductance). If a noisy current, such as an LED being multiplexed, a processor, or a display, returns through the same piece of ground wire as an audio signal's reference, the voltage that current makes across the shared wire appears in the audio:

```formula
V_noise = I_noisy R_shared
V_noise = 0.1 A × 0.05 Ω = 0.005 V = 5 mV
where
V_noise: the voltage added to the audio's ground reference, in volts (V)
I_noisy: the noisy return current sharing the wire, here 100 mA = 0.1 amperes (A) of LED current
R_shared: the resistance of the shared stretch of ground wire, here 0.05 ohms (Ω)
V: volts
A: amperes
Ω: ohms
mV: millivolts; 1 mV = 0.001 V
In words: 100 mA of LED current through a twentieth of an ohm of shared wire shifts the audio's ground by 5 mV, in step with the LEDs. This is a 5 mV reference shift. If an unwanted variation is 5 mV RMS, its level is roughly 36 dB below a 0.316 V RMS signal; audibility depends on gain, spectrum and listening conditions. The LED-current magnitude alone does not specify its noise RMS level.
```

The figures are illustrative; the fix is to stop the noisy current sharing the wire at all.

```diagram
 BAD: daisy-chained ground
 audio ──┬── LEDs ──┬── MCU ──┬── supply −
         └ shared wire carries all returns

 GOOD: star ground
          audio   LEDs    MCU
            │       │      │
            └───────┼──────┘
                    ● star point
                    │
                supply −
```

**Star grounding** (single-point grounding) at an introductory level means:

- Each sub-circuit has its own return wire to one common point.
- High-current and noisy returns don't share wire with sensitive audio returns.
- The star point is usually at the power entry or where the audio reference is defined.

You won't build perfect stars on a breadboard. Apply the principle with intent: give the audio output's ground its own wire back to the board's ground pin, and keep LED and motor returns off it.

## Analogue and digital ground
Boards with audio codecs often talk about **AGND** (analogue ground) and **DGND** (digital ground). At a conceptual level:

- Digital circuits produce large, fast, spiky return currents.
- Analogue audio needs a quiet, stable reference.
- Layout keeps noisy digital return currents away from sensitive analogue references. Often this uses careful placement over a **continuous ground plane**; a split plane or one-point join is not a universal requirement.

Two cautions:

- **Use the specified grounding topology.** AGND and DGND must have the connection required by the manufacturer, often both directly to one low-impedance plane. Splitting that plane or forcing a distant single-point join can worsen high-frequency current return paths.
- **Follow the manufacturer.** If your audio board exposes separate analogue and digital ground pins, connect pots, audio jacks and analogue parts as its documentation directs. Codec datasheets specify their own grounding and layout. This is advanced material; for the first build, follow the board's guidance and keep noisy and quiet wiring physically apart.

## Key takeaways

- Separate noisy return currents from sensitive references.
- Follow the board’s grounding topology; a split plane is not universal.

## Further reading

- [Analog Devices MT-031: converter grounding](https://www.analog.com/media/en/training-seminars/tutorials/MT-031.pdf)
- [RaneNote 110: system interconnection](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/note110.html)

options.explanation: Never lift an earth. And the symptom here, a buzz tracking the LEDs, points to shared impedance inside the build.

options.text: The LEDs emit light that the audio circuit picks up
options.explanation: Optical coupling isn't the cause. The coupling is electrical, through the ground wire.

options.text: Shared-impedance coupling: LED return current through the shared wire's resistance shifts the audio ground. Give the audio its own return to a star point
options.explanation: Correct. The LED current times the shared wire's resistance appears in the audio reference. Separate returns to a single point stop the LED current flowing in the audio ground.

options.text: The audio output needs a larger output capacitor
options.explanation: That wouldn't stop LED current flowing in the audio ground reference.

questions.workedExample:
1. A daisy-chained ground carries every sub-circuit's return current through common sections.
2. The LED current switches on and off in the LED pattern. Through the shared wire's resistance it creates a varying voltage.
3. The audio stage's ground reference moves by that voltage, so you hear the LED pattern.
4. Star grounding: each sub-circuit returns on its own wire to one point. LED current then never flows in the audio return.

questions.prompt: An audio board exposes separate AGND and DGND pins. Which approach best matches standard practice at a conceptual level?

options.text: Leave AGND and DGND unconnected so digital noise can't reach analogue
options.explanation: Without a connection the two halves have no common reference, and signals between them return through unintended paths. That usually makes noise worse.

options.text: Follow the manufacturer's grounding layout and keep noisy return currents away from sensitive analogue references
options.explanation: Correct. The recommended solution may be a continuous plane or a specified join; AGND/DGND labels alone do not require separate ground regions.

options.text: Join arbitrary ground points without checking the board layout or return-current paths
options.explanation: Random wiring is not a grounding design. Multiple low-impedance connections can be correct on a common plane, but must follow the documented layout.

options.text: Connect analogue parts to DGND because it has more pins
options.explanation: Pin count is irrelevant. Analogue parts belong on the analogue return, as the documentation specifies.

questions.workedExample: AGND and DGND labels identify pin functions, not a universal split-ground rule. Consult the codec and board documentation. A continuous low-impedance plane with suitable placement often gives the best current return paths; a split or distant single join can force noisy currents on a detour. Connect external pots and jacks as the board requires.

lessons.title: Shielding, twisted pairs and balanced audio
lessons.summary: Connector shape alone does not establish balanced operation.
lessons.body:
Connector shape alone does not establish balanced operation.

## Shielded cable and wiring
A **shielded cable** surrounds the signal conductor(s) with a braid or foil connected to ground. The shield intercepts electric-field interference before it reaches the signal.

- **Unbalanced (TS):** one conductor plus shield. The shield is also the signal return, so ground-loop current in it adds to the signal.
- **Balanced wiring (often TRS or XLR):** two signal conductors plus shield. The shield is not the intended audio signal-return conductor, and interference common to both conductors cancels at a balanced input.
- **Twisting** a signal wire with its return reduces magnetic pickup, because each twist reverses the induced voltage.

Inside the build:

- Keep audio wires short and away from digital lines, LED wiring and power.
- Cross noisy wiring at right angles rather than running it alongside audio.
- Run each signal and its own return together.

## Check function as well as connector

A TRS connector may carry unbalanced stereo, balanced mono or another function. It does not make a circuit balanced. A balanced interface needs suitably balanced impedances to ground and a differential receiver with adequate common-mode rejection and input range. Its two output voltages need not always be equal and opposite. Follow both devices’ actual wiring documentation.

## Key takeaways

- Connector shape alone does not establish balanced operation.
- Keep signals close to their own returns and away from noise sources.

## Further reading

- [RaneNote 110: system interconnection](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/note110.html)
- [Analog Devices MT-095: interference and shielding](https://www.analog.com/media/en/training-seminars/tutorials/MT-095.pdf)

questions.prompt: What does the shield of an unbalanced (TS) audio cable do?

options.text: Nothing electrical; it only adds strength
options.explanation: The shield is electrically essential: it intercepts interference and is the signal's current return path.

options.text: It carries the signal; the inner conductor is the ground
options.explanation: The inner conductor (tip) carries the signal. The shield (sleeve) is ground.

options.text: It must be disconnected at both ends
options.explanation: A shield disconnected at both ends does nothing, and an unbalanced cable would lose its current return path entirely.

options.text: It intercepts electric-field interference and also carries the signal's return current
options.explanation: Correct. In an unbalanced cable the shield is both screen and return conductor, which is why ground-loop current in it adds directly to the audio.

questions.workedExample:
1. A TS cable has a tip (signal) and a sleeve (shield/ground).
2. The shield surrounds the tip conductor, catching interference and draining it to ground.
3. It's also the current return path for the signal current.
4. Any other current in the shield, such as ground-loop current, creates a voltage drop that adds to the signal. That's the unbalanced connection's weakness.

questions.prompt: Which wiring practice inside a synth housing best reduces noise pickup on an audio line?

options.text: Keep audio wires short, run each signal with its own return (twisted if possible), and route them away from digital and power wiring, crossing at right angles
options.explanation: Correct. Short, twisted pairs routed away from noisy lines reduce both electric and magnetic pickup.

options.text: Bundle audio wires tightly with LED and digital wires to keep things tidy
options.explanation: Running audio alongside noisy wiring maximises coupling between them.

options.text: Use the longest wires possible so they can be moved later
options.explanation: Longer wires form bigger loops and antennas, which pick up more noise.

options.text: Route the audio signal and its ground on opposite sides of the board
options.explanation: Separating a signal from its return enlarges the loop area, which increases magnetic pickup.

questions.workedExample:
1. Pickup depends on proximity to noise sources and on loop area.
2. Keep signal and return together, twisted, to minimise loop area.
3. Keep the run short.
4. Route audio wiring separately from digital and power wiring, and cross at right angles when you must.

questions.prompt: Why does a balanced connection reject ground-loop hum that an unbalanced one passes?

options.text: Balanced cables use thicker shields
options.explanation: Shield thickness helps a little, but rejection comes from the differential input.

options.text: Balanced signals are digital
options.explanation: Balanced audio is analogue. It's a wiring and input technique.

options.text: The differential receiver measures two signal conductors; equal common-mode noise cancels ideally, and the shield is not the intended signal return
options.explanation: Correct. Balanced impedances to ground and a differential receiver reduce common-mode interference. Actual rejection is finite and requires the receiver’s input range and the equipment wiring to be respected.

options.text: Balanced connections remove the need for ground
options.explanation: There's still a shield and a ground reference. They just aren't in the signal path.

questions.workedExample:
1. Compare what each kind of input actually measures when hum adds the same unwanted voltage to the conductors:

```formula
V_in = V_tip − V_shield
V_in = V_tip − (0 V + V_n) = V_tip − V_n
V_in = (V_hot + V_n) − (V_cold + V_n)
V_in = V_hot − V_cold
where
V: volts, the unit of voltage
V_in: the voltage the receiving input amplifies, in volts (V). The first two lines are an unbalanced (TS) input, which measures the tip against the shield; the last two are a balanced input, which measures hot against cold
V_tip: the signal conductor's voltage, in volts
V_shield: the shield's voltage at the receiving end, in volts; ideally 0 V, but loop current adds V_n to it
V_n: the unwanted voltage from loop current or interference, in volts
V_hot: the voltage on the hot conductor, in volts
V_cold: the voltage on the cold conductor, in volts
In words: an unbalanced input measures against the shield, so any hum voltage on the shield goes straight into the audio. A balanced input subtracts cold from hot, so hum that appears equally on both cancels out.
```

2. Interference and ground shifts appear nearly equally on hot and cold (common-mode), so the difference cancels them.
3. The shield is not the intended audio signal-return conductor; leakage, interference and other unwanted currents may still flow in it.
4. Rejection depends on impedance balance and the differential receiver; equal-and-opposite output voltages are not essential. In practice the cancellation is large but never perfect.

lessons.title: Supply noise, rejection and a diagnostic checklist
lessons.summary: Compare supplies methodically and follow documented decoupling and filtering.
lessons.body:
Compare supplies methodically and follow documented decoupling and filtering.

## Power supply noise and decoupling
A synth's supply often comes from a computer's USB port or a USB charger. Both carry noise: digital load current from the computer, and supply ripple at the supply-switching rate of switch-mode chargers and regulators.

How it reaches the audio:

- Op-amps, codecs and regulators reject supply noise only partially. Their **power supply rejection ratio (PSRR)** typically falls as frequency rises, so high-frequency supply noise gets through more easily. Datasheets show this as a "PSRR vs frequency" graph; TI’s OPA1612 datasheet SBOS450C (revision C, August 2014; checked 16 October 2026) has an example (its "CMRR and PSRR vs Frequency" figure).
- Digital chips on the same rail inject current spikes, which the local decoupling capacitors described earlier help contain.

Defences, in order of effort:

1. **Follow each chip’s decoupling requirements** with short supply paths and current return paths, plus specified bulk storage at power entry. 100 nF is the SN74HC00 example, not a universal bill of materials.
2. **Filter the analogue supply** from the digital one with a small resistor or inductor and a capacitor (an RC or LC low-pass, the component units).
3. **Use a dedicated low-noise linear regulator** for analogue parts, if the board design calls for it.
4. **Use a better source:** try a different USB supply or a battery bank to see whether the noise follows the supply.

Audio-focused development boards often build these measures in. Read the board's documentation before adding your own. Your main job is not to undo them with poor external wiring.

## A noise-hunting checklist
- Identify the noise: steady 50/100 Hz hum (ground loop or mains field), or whine that tracks computer, LED or processor activity (digital ground or supply noise).
- Remove connections one at a time and note what changes.
- Try battery power for the synth.
- Check that audio grounds return directly to the board's ground, not through LED or digital wiring.
- Confirm decoupling capacitors are present and close to their pins.
- Use balanced or isolated connections between devices where possible.
- Never remove a mains safety earth.

## Key takeaways

- Compare supplies methodically and follow documented decoupling and filtering.
- A battery test implicates changed paths; it does not prove a unique cause.

## Further reading

- [Analog Devices MT-101: decoupling techniques](https://www.analog.com/media/en/training-seminars/tutorials/MT-101.pdf)
- [TI OPA1612: PSRR versus frequency](https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/opa1612.pdf)
- [Analog Devices MT-031: converter grounding](https://www.analog.com/media/en/training-seminars/tutorials/MT-031.pdf)

questions.prompt: Your synth's audio output has a faint high-pitched whine that disappears when you power the board from a battery bank instead of a USB wall charger. Which explanations and remedies are reasonable? Select all that apply.

options.text: The whine is caused by the battery being too weak
options.explanation: The whine disappears on the battery, so the battery isn't the cause.

options.text: The charger's switch-mode ripple reaches the audio because the circuit's PSRR is limited, especially at higher frequencies
options.explanation: Correct. Switch-mode supplies produce ripple at their supply-switching rate, and supply rejection typically weakens as frequency rises.

options.text: Add or improve decoupling and filtering on the analogue supply (for example an RC or LC low-pass)
options.explanation: Correct. It reduces how much ripple reaches the sensitive parts.

options.text: Try a different, cleaner USB supply
options.explanation: Correct. Supplies vary widely in noise, so swapping is a quick test and may be a fix.

questions.workedExample:
1. The power-source change implicates the supply arrangement, but can also change ground paths and coupling. It does not prove ripple is the unique cause.
2. Switch-mode chargers produce ripple at their supply-switching rate (and sometimes audible sub-harmonics under light load).
3. Op-amps, codecs and regulators reject supply noise imperfectly. PSRR typically falls with frequency.
4. Remedies: a better supply, local decoupling, an RC/LC filter or linear regulator on the analogue rail, and follow the board's power guidance.
